title: Vianode seeks partner for cooperation or acquisition - electrive.com
content:
Norwegian battery materials specialist Vianode is seeking a partner for its next expansion phase. According to CEO Burkhard Straube, the company is open to various options, ranging from cooperation to a full acquisition.
Image: Vianode
Vianode is a Norwegian specialist in synthetic graphite and has been operating its first large-scale production facility, named ‘Via One’, in Herøya, Norway, since 2024. According to the company, this is “the world’s most sustainable synthetic anode graphite plant”. Vianode has been producing the material since 2021, initially using a pilot plant in Kristiansand.
Since the end of 2025
, Vianode has also been constructing a second plant in St. Thomas, in the Canadian province of Ontario. The facility is set to be located near Volkswagen’s PowerCo plant and is referred to by the Norwegians as ‘Via Two’.
However, GM is considered the anchor customer there
rather than Volkswagen.
As CEO Burkhard Straube recently told
, Vianode is now reaching its limits and will need support in the future. The company is therefore looking for a partner who can contribute capital, industrial expertise, or broader strategic collaboration for the next phase of expansion. Straube told the news agency that Vianode is open to various options, ranging from a partnership to a full acquisition, and specified that the company has engaged JP Morgan to assist with the process.
According to
, the Swedish private equity firm Altor has been Vianode’s sole funder since 2024. The previous investor, Norsk Hydro, withdrew as a shareholder at that time. The agency report now states that Vianode hopes to find a partner by the end of this year. The company is one of the few non-Asian players in the production of synthetic graphite.
adds that China controls approximately 95 per cent of the global supply of battery-grade graphite.
Straube is convinced that customers also have an interest in a strong supplier. Altor spokesperson Andreas Hamrin added: “It is an attractive case for the right partner, with Vianode having proven both its technological and commercial viability.”
Once fully ramped up, Vianode’s Norwegian plant is expected to produce around 2,000 tonnes of graphite battery material annually – enough for approximately 35,000 electric vehicles. However, in 2023, the company shifted its expansion focus to North America, where, at that time under US President Joe Biden, there were greater incentives and regulatory support. Production there is currently scheduled to begin in 2029 – significantly later than originally planned.

title: T&E analysis: sufficient European battery cells by 2030 - electrive.com
content:
In an analysis of the EU's planned local content requirements for batteries, T&E has concluded that a sufficient number of 'Made in EU' battery cells will be available by 2030. This contradicts the current claims of the automotive industry.
View inside CATL's battery factory in Arnstadt
Image: CATL
For months, the EU and its member states have been discussing
draft proposals
for the ‘Industrial Accelerator Act’ (IAA) introduced in March, which aims to boost production and competitiveness within the European Union. These measures also affect the automotive and battery industries: for example, the European Commission plans to introduce so-called Local Content provisions that would prioritise ‘Made in EU’ EVs – i.e., those manufactured within the EU – in public procurement and funding programmes.
Special conditions for local value creation in the EU are also envisaged for traction batteries in electric vehicles. This has recently caused significant concern, as the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA) has
examining whether the European battery supply chain can meet the requirements of the legislative package. The result: a significant gap. ACEA argues that there is a time lag: a new battery factory can take nearly a decade from announcement to full-scale industrial production. Even projects launched today may not reach full capacity until around 2035. ACEA is therefore calling for more time and a phased introduction of Local Content requirements, particularly for cells and cathode active materials.
European battery cell production to meet demand by 2030
However, the think tank Transport & Environment (T&E) has now presented its own study, concluding that sufficient ‘Made in EU’ battery cells will be available by 2030. T&E itself emphasises that the analysis contradicts the recent claims of the automotive industry – namely, those of ACEA.
According to the study, European cell production will already be sufficient by 2027 to fully cover the demand for funded company cars and a significant portion of funded private cars. By 2030, both segments could be supplied with enough European battery cells – provided that projects with a medium probability of implementation are also realised. However, a quarter of the cell capacities announced since 2022 have been cancelled or put on hold. Germany is particularly affected, with its project pipeline for 2035 halved, according to T&E. The organisation cites examples such as
ACC in Kaiserslautern
closure of Cellforce by Porsche
. On the other hand, VW subsidiary PowerCo was able to open its
first cell factory in Salzgitter
in December 2025, which, once ramped up, will significantly increase local value creation in the battery supply chain.
Notably, the ownership structure of European cell production is also striking: according to T&E, more than 85 per cent of active capacity is owned by non-European companies, with South Korean manufacturers accounting for 72 per cent of production. The South Korean manufacturers in question are likely LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI, and SK On, which operate cell factories in Poland and Hungary, respectively. Another major cell manufacturer is the Chinese battery giant CATL, with its
factory in Arnstadt near Erfurt
and its second European factory in Debrecen, Hungary, which has just
started test production
For the ‘Made in EU’ requirements, it is the production location rather than the manufacturer’s country of origin that matters. In other words, the establishment of Asian battery cell manufacturers in the EU also helps meet the Local Content criteria, as local production within the EU is the decisive factor.
“Since the collapse of Northvolt, there has been considerable scepticism in Germany about whether it is possible to build a domestic battery industry. Yet our data shows that Germany is already a relevant location in the European battery ecosystem and has great potential. When Berlin debates the future of German industry, much of the focus is on products of the past, such as the internal combustion engine. It is time to shift the focus to industries of the future, like the battery industry. Supporting an effective Industry Accelerator Act would be an important step here,” said Susanne Goetz, Senior Advisor for E-Mobility at T&E Germany.
Xavier Sol, Director Sustainable Investments and Batteries at T&E, added: “Recent years have shown that, unfortunately, a strong European battery value chain won’t build itself – the competition from Asia is simply too large. Without smart demand-side rules for locally produced battery components, Europe risks its qualification in the race for clean tech. Building a secure, local value chain can ensure security of supply, create jobs and economic resilience”
T&E identifies larger gaps in precursor materials. For cathode active material (CAM), although 529,000 tonnes of annual European capacity have been announced for 2030, only around 177,000 tonnes remain after weighting projects by their probability of implementation. The uncertainty is even greater for pCAM (cathode precursor material): of the announced projects with a total of 552.6 GWh cell equivalent, T&E considers only 217.9 GWh likely to be achieved by 2030. The organisation therefore advocates maintaining the planned cell and CAM requirements of the Industry Accelerator Act and, in addition, introducing minimum quotas for pCAM and anode active material from 2032 onwards.

title: How 587 Cells Redefine Utility-Scale Battery Storage Efficiency
content:
Lithium-Ion Batteries
Battery Manufacturing
Market Analysis
Industry Trends
Discover how 587 cells revolutionize utility-scale battery storage with higher efficiency, fewer components, and optimized system performance.
September 30, 2026
5 Min Read
Production line of 587 Ah cells.
Courtesy of HiTHIUM.
Eight years ago, a standard 20-foot battery container shipped with 3.72 MWh inside. Today, the same container holds 6.25 MWh. Some incremental chemistry gains played into this jump, but simple geometry was the main driver: manufacturers optimized cell design to pack more capacity into the same footprint.
Integrator roadmaps have largely settled on 587Ah, but the installed base has not. Cells of 500Ah and above passed 10% penetration in utility-scale storage in the first half of 2026; 314 Ah still ships most of the volume and has been in tight supply for nearly a year, with prices up more than 15% over six months.
Large-format LFP cells grew from 280Ah in 2018 to 314 Ah in 2023 to 587Ah in 2026. Logistics, safety, and system integration constraints shaped this progression as much as any advancement in materials, and developers who treat it as a spec race may not understand how it affects project outcomes.
Related:
Growing Role of LFP Batteries in Global Energy Transition
TENER Sodium Energy Storage System. Courtesy of CATL.
Why 587Ah leads right now
Larger cells remain technically possible; cells above 1,000Ah already exist. But 587Ah sits where three fixed constraints intersect:
The cell stack fits a 20-foot ISO shipping container
The loaded container remains under the 45-tonne road transport limitations
The system operates within the 1,500 VDC ceiling of most utility-scale inverters
Compared with the 314Ah generation, a 587Ah container delivers 25% more energy (kWh) with 40% fewer parts. CATL published data last year showing total system components fell from roughly 30,000 to 18,000.
Every eliminated welding point, Battery Management System node, and assembly step removes cost and a potential early-life failure point. Fewer cells per container also means fewer hotspots for the thermal management system to track. CATL, REPT, and Hithium all sell this format today, which suggests the underlying math looks similar across manufacturers.
CATL leads with 587Ah and positions it as a broadly compatible standard tied to its Tener 6.25 MWh family; REPT, CALB, Cornex, and Sunwoda are pushing 588 as the more aggressive long-duration option.
Manufacturers keep pushing
The size race hasn't stopped at 587Ah. Hithium built its 1,175Ah and 1,300Ah cells from a clean design for 4- to 8-hour long-duration storage, rather than scaling up a 2-hour cell. The 1,300Ah version, the first dedicated 8-hour storage cell, enters mass production in the fourth quarter of 2026. It delivers more than four times the capacity of mainstream products while cutting component count by more than 30%.
Hithium 1,300Ah cells designed for 6.9MWh BESS. Courtesy of Hithium.
This bet assumes grid energy-to-power ratios will keep increasing as solar and wind penetration continue to grow. BYD sits at the far end of the spectrum with its 2,710Ah Blade cell. The system built around it delivers at least 14.5MWh per container, more than double Tesla's Megapack 3.
Related:
Q&A: Standardized Imaging Framework Enhances Battery Research Reliability
However, at this concentration, thermal management goes from a standard engineering exercise to a first-of-its-kind challenge. Independent safety data for the format remains limited, partly because BYD sells integrated systems rather than standalone cells, which limits buyers' visibility into cell-level specifications.
Large-format cells are energy cells, and the fastest-growing new demand segment is moving the opposite way. Great Power introduced an 85Ah cell for data center use designed for 10C discharge and millisecond response, and Narada showed a backup platform above 600kW per cabinet with high pulse capability.
The grid isn't converging on one cell size because it isn't converging on one duty cycle.
The trade-offs developers need to weigh
With the sticker price of a larger cell, several recurring costs are not immediately obvious and are hidden in ongoing operations that may be harder to estimate.
A container of 314Ah cells runs on roughly 60 kW of liquid cooling; a container of 587Ah cells needs about 80kW. This 33% jump forces new cooling system designs, higher engineering spend, and site-specific thermal analysis the previous generation never required. Auxiliary cooling load is parasitic draw against round-trip efficiency for the life of the asset, not just a capex line. On a multi-hundred-container project, this cost compounds fast.
Related:
Donut Lab Battery Breakdown Highlights Importance of Independent Testing
Cell failures are also more concerning. Larger cells concentrate more energy in a single failure point, raising short-circuit and arc-fault exposure. Peer-reviewed modeling puts thermal runaway in starker terms: cells above 600Ah may eject more than 2 kg of electrolyte per cell during a runaway event, roughly double the 314Ah baseline.
Most fire suppression systems in the field carry certifications built for smaller formats, and those systems haven’t yet demonstrated whether they can handle the larger cells. Not to mention, NFPA 855’s 2026 edition moved Large-Scale Fire Testing (LSFT) from optional to expected, which is also a reason why integrator queues are long right now.
Manufacturers present volumetric density as a headline achievement, and more energy in the same space sounds like pure upside. But higher density also concentrates heat, with key engineering trade-offs: thinner separators between electrode layers, tighter cell-to-cell spacing with less room for airflow, or cathode formulations boosting energy content at the cost of thermal stability margin.
A cell at 450Wh/L carries different cooling, layout, and insurance requirements than one at 430Wh/L. Before picking the highest number on a datasheet, ask what got traded away to produce it.
How to choose a cell size in 2026
The 587Ah format marks the intersection where physics, logistics, and system economics line up today, but it may not remain the best choice for all projects forever.
Larger formats bring real advantages: fewer components, higher energy density, and storage durations fitting the long-duration profiles the grid increasingly demands. They also pose safety questions that fire suppression standards haven't caught up to, and qualification timelines longer than most development schedules assume.
Cell selection should be a system-level decision: verify integrator qualification status, engineer site-specific thermal requirements, and negotiate contract terms holding the manufacturer to its performance claims.
Here’s a simple checklist one should consider when evaluating BESS:
Which formats have completed full qualification?
At what level, when, and where was this cell-and-enclosure combination fire tested?
Cycle life is anchored to what state of health, C-rate, and temperature range?
What is the container's auxiliary load, and does the round-trip efficiency guarantee sit above or below it?
What is the gravimetric density in Wh/kg?
What is the augmentation path and spare parts strategy going forward?
For US-based projects, what Foreign Entity of Concern documentation exists?
What kind of insurance (or re-insurance) is being carried by the integrator on the product?
Developers should pick the cell your project can build around, not the one with the biggest number on the spec sheet.
About the Author
Raafe Khan
Head of Energy Storage and Emerging Markets , Camelot Energy Group
Raafe Khan is Camelot's Head of Energy Storage and Emerging Markets at Camelot Energy Group. He is a recipient of several national and international awards, including being a Forbes Under 30 honoree in the field of energy. An ardent advocate for energy access and equity, he is an accredited lecturer for the Battery MBA program and devotes his time to educating stakeholders in the energy storage space about technical and commercial challenges from the cell to a fully functional container system. Raafe has a Bachelor's in Electrical & Electronics Engineering degree from Manipal University and a Master's in Energy Science, Technology & Public Policy from Carnegie Mellon University.

Leaders gathered at Supply Chain LIVE to discuss the latest burning topics
Supply chain leaders from around the world joined together at the Queen Elizabeth II Centre in London for two days of networking and collaboration
The last few years have seen tremendous changes to how supply chains around the world operate, driven by ongoing volatility, climate disruption and tariff threats. Supply chain executives gathered in London for Supply Chain LIVE, a two-day event taking place alongside Procurement LIVE, Manufacturing LIVE and Sustainability LIVE at the QEII Centre, tackling the main challenges and most innovative solutions.
Leaders took to the Supply Chain Stage to discuss the role of AI in the supply chain, the growing influence of sustainability targets and
emerging resilience strategies
Attendees heard keynote speeches delivered by Kim Faulkner from Tate & Lyle, Alexander Tschentscher of Siemens, Aurelien Faucheux from Bugatti Rimac, Maiya Shibasaki from Hitachi Rail, Stephen Carter of Ivalua and Steffen Lang from Novartis. With 2,500 attendees, Supply Chain LIVE was the perfect place for leaders to network, with four floors open to executives across procurement, sustainability and manufacturing.
The two-day event helped spark new conversations, offered key insights into innovative ways of thinking and helped motivate leaders to transform their supply chain operations.
Around the world, supply chain decision-makers have been forced to adapt to ongoing disruption. During times of volatility, it is important to celebrate those redefining progress.
On 8 September, the
Global Supply Chain Awards
were held at JW Marriott Grosvenor House, bringing leaders together for a black-tie gala dinner. The awards celebrated the individuals and organisations integrating sustainability and technology into their operations to drive change.
Held alongside the Global Procurement Awards and the Global Sustainability Awards, the evening served as the perfect opportunity to champion innovation and inspire other leaders to drive supply chain success.

title: Mondelēz Canada Invests in Sustainable Supply Chains
content:
Mondelēz Canada Invests in Sustainable Supply Chains
Prioritise Us
on Google
Mondelēz Canada is supporting Canadian farmers and strengthening agricultural supply chain resilience. Credit: Getty Images
Mondelēz Canada invests in Area One Farms Fund V to develop a resilient Canadian food system, Naniss Gadel-Raab, President, Mondelēz Canada explains
Mondelēz Canada is investing in Area One Farms Fund V to strengthen Canadian agricultural supply chain resilience and support farmers in the transition to regenerative agriculture.
The investment, made through Mondelēz International's Sustainable Futures Impact Investment platform alongside impact investment firm Sagana, will provide growth capital to family farms across Canada.
The initiative aims to
reinforce supply chain infrastructure
Area One Farms partners with farmers to expand operations while maintaining farmer participation in land ownership.
Capital access for supply chains
Area One Farms works with growth-oriented Canadian family farms that have opportunities to expand but may face challenges accessing the capital required to do so. Through its partnership model, farmers and Area One Farms invest alongside one another, sharing the financial outcomes of the farm's performance.
Funding can support the acquisition of additional land, improvements to underproductive or retired farmland and investment in infrastructure, machinery and precision agriculture technology. The model is designed to strengthen the financial foundations of farming businesses while supporting increased agricultural production.
Investment in farm infrastructure and equipment could mean greater capacity to
supply food manufacturers
with consistent volumes. The model also supports the working capital and equipment needed to adopt locally appropriate regenerative agriculture practices, while sharing some of the financial cost and risk of that transition.
"Farmers are core to this transition (scaling regenerative agriculture), but they can't do it alone," says Christine Montenegro McGrath, SVP and Chief Impact & Sustainability Officer, Mondelēz International, on LinkedIn.
Christine Montenegro McGrath, SVP and Chief Impact & Sustainability Officer, Mondelēz International
"They're facing changing growing conditions, rising costs and the risk of adopting new practices. We need models that work across farming systems and geographies, delivering value for farmers while strengthening supply chains."
Key numbers
Mondelēz sources approximately 100% of its cocoa volume for chocolate brands through its Cocoa Life programme
It works with more than 257,000 registered farmers across the project
Mondelēz has made approximately 60% progress towards its 2030 GHG reduction target against its 2018 baseline
Around 96% of its total packaging is designed to be recyclable, with the company targeting 98% by 2030
The company has reduced its overall virgin plastic use by 11.5% compared with 2020 levels
Supply chain resilience through ownership
The partnership model seeks to help family farms grow while maintaining farmers' participation in land ownership across generations. Rather than following conventional farmland investment models based on investors acquiring land and charging farmers fixed rent, Area One Farms enables farmers to retain an ownership interest in the farm partnership.
Farmers can also have a pathway to increase their stake over time as the partnership develops. This structure is intended to give farming families greater opportunity to scale their operations while preserving their connection to the land.
"Most farmers who want to grow are not
short of skill or opportunity
. They are short of growth equity," says Joelle Faulkner, CEO at Area One Farms.
Joelle Faulkner, CEO at Area One Farms
"We invest as a co-owner, supporting them with capital and mentorship to scale and innovate. Mondelēz understands that a resilient supply chain starts on farms that are financially strong enough to invest in their soil and in the next generation and this investment lets us do that work with more farming families across Canada."
Supporting the next generation of farmers is relevant as agricultural businesses face pressure to invest in technology, infrastructure and more resilient production systems. These investments could show benefits for supply chain continuity as farms maintain operations across generational transitions.
We know that investing in Canadian agriculture helps strengthen the foundation of a resilient Canadian food system and the agricultural supply chains that are essential to food manufacturing in Canada.
Naniss Gadel-Raab, President, Mondelēz Canada
Financing sustainable supply chain practices
Alongside growth capital, Area One Farms can provide funding for the equipment and working capital needed to
adopt regenerative agriculture practices
. Farmers can receive agronomic support while implementing approaches such as reduced tillage and cover cropping, helping to address some of the financial barriers associated with changing farming practices.
The strategy can also support initiatives focused on improving soil health, increasing input efficiency, managing water resources and strengthening resilience to climate-related pressures. By sharing some of the costs and risks associated with the transition, the partnership model can give farmers greater capacity to invest in longer-term land management.
"As a company, we know that investing in Canadian agriculture helps strengthen the foundation of a resilient Canadian food system and the agricultural supply chains that are essential to food manufacturing in Canada," says Naniss Gadel-Raab, President, Mondelēz Canada.
Naniss Gadel-Rab, President of Mondelēz Canada
"Our commitment to Canada extends beyond the products we make; it includes supporting the farmers, families and communities that are helping build a
stronger, more sustainable food system
These locally appropriate practices are intended to support productive farmland while improving the environmental resilience of agricultural operations. Mondelēz Canada's investment connects access to capital with the longer-term resilience of the food system and the communities that depend on agriculture.
Expanding infrastructure across Canadian farmland
According to Area One Farms, the organisation has grown to more than C$800m in assets under management across more than 50 farm partnerships and 200,000 acres, building its model through four previous funds. Mondelēz Canada's investment in Fund V will support the expansion of this approach and enable Area One Farms to partner with additional farming families across Canada.
The investment is intended to support increased crop production while
advancing regenerative agriculture
practices suited to local farming conditions. For Mondelēz Canada, strengthening agricultural supply chains is connected to supporting the farmers and communities that supply ingredients and materials to the food manufacturing sector.
The initiative demonstrates how investment capital can be directed towards both the economic resilience of farming businesses and the longer-term sustainability of Canada's agricultural landscape.
"We have a playbook and enough demonstration that regenerative agriculture works, but financing the transition remains a big barrier," says François Ritchot, Investment Director and Food & Agriculture Lead at Sagana.
François Ritchot, Investment Director and Food & Agriculture Lead at Sagana
"Area One Farms offers a distinctive approach to address this. We were particularly attracted by the combination of disciplined real-asset investing, practical regenerative agriculture capabilities and tangible benefits for farming families, rural communities and the resilience of our food system."
Companies and partnerships

World Cocoa Foundation

Founded by Adam Metz, the firm takes a patient, concentrated approach to investing, often holding positions for extended periods. Sagana emphasizes fundamental analysis and works closely with management teams. The firm is known for its low-profile operation and disciplined investment philosophy, targeting businesses with strong competitive advantages and sustainable growth potential.

title: Ford's $30,000 Fathom EV pickup production launch faces uncertainty [Update]
content:
Peter Johnson
| Oct 1 2026 - 7:37 am PT
Ford Fathom
is expected to go on sale in early 2027, starting at $28,350. Ford CEO Jim Farley admitted, “It’s going to be a heck of an effort to launch this at scale, at cost, on time.”
Ford Fathom production still faces hurdles
After Ford said just last month it was
on track to begin Fathom production
in 2027, that timeline is now facing uncertainty.
Speaking at the
2026 Automotive News Congress
this week, Ford CEO Jim Farley explained how its Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) platform could be the automaker’s answer to Chinese brands like BYD, which are rapidly gaining market share in Europe and other key global markets.
Farley said the company realized at one point that a BYD EV would have roughly a 20% cost advantage over Fathom’s battery.
To stay competitive, the team modified the motors, gearboxes, and inverters, enabling smaller batteries than BYD’s.
While it sounds promising, Farley admitted that “It’s going to be a heck of an effort to launch this at scale, at cost, on time.”
Ford Fathom EV pickup prototype (Source: Jim Farley)
Farley added that “We haven’t landed the plane on mass production of UEV yet.” Ford previously said the first Fathom prototypes are scheduled to roll off the assembly line at its 3-million-square-foot Louisville Assembly Plant (LAP) in 2027.
Ford is investing $5 billion between its Louisville Assembly Plant and BlueOval Battery Park in Michigan to prepare for UEV production.
Covered Ford Fathom vehicle (Source: Ford)
According to a recent
Wall Street Journal
report citing sources familiar with the matter, Ford aims to sell 100,000 Fathoms in its first year. With UEV production hurdles persisting, that might be hard to hit.
When it goes on sale, still expected in early 2027 until Ford confirms otherwise, the Fathom will start at $28,350 for the standard range battery model.
Update 10/01/2026:
A Ford spokesperson told
Electrek
, “We’ve said previously, ‘Fathom will launch in 2027 ‘- and there is no change to that.”
Ford’s midsize UEV pickup spotted charging at a Tesla Supercharger (Source: Reddit)
Farley previously said the Fathom will offer more interior passenger space than a Toyota RAV4. It will also be the first to have
Apple Maps integrated
directly into the navigation system, a “large touchscreen display,” wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, BlueCruise, bidirectional charging capabilities, and a digital key.
We also know the electric pickup will have a NACS port after a few prototypes were
spotted charging at a Tesla Supercharger
this summer.

title: Aptera (SEV) now says it needs $25M to start production, stock drops 15%
content:
Aptera (SEV) now says it needs only about $25 million to start production of its Solar EV, down from the $40 to $45 million it quoted just seven weeks ago.
It’s good news on paper. But the market didn’t buy it: Aptera’s stock fell about 15% on the announcement, leaving the solar car startup with a market cap of roughly $69 million.
A smaller number, same problem
In its Q2 2026 results in August, Aptera said it needed $40 to $45 million to launch low-volume production at its Carlsbad facility, plus another $140 to $160 million to reach high volume.
The new plan, published today, is a lot leaner:
- About $25 million to start production, with the first 40 vehicles built starting by the end of 2026
- $40 million more to ramp to 500 vehicles per month, which Aptera calls self-sustaining
- $50 million more for high-volume tooling, targeting about 20,000 vehicles a year
That’s roughly $115 million all-in, compared to $180 to $205 million before. Aptera credits its recent partnership with Launch Design, design-for-manufacturing changes, international suppliers, and a bill of materials updated with actual supplier quotes.
“This is a fundamentally leaner path to getting Aptera into customers’ hands,” said co-CEO Chris Anthony.
Customer deliveries are now pegged for early 2027, “subject to financing.”
The goalposts keep moving
We’ve heard versions of this before. In late 2024, Aptera was trying to raise $60 million to reach low-volume production and called its delivery timeline a “moving target.” Back then, the first 60 Launch Edition cars were supposed to ship in 2025.
In January, after a $9 million public offering at $2 per share, the company was still targeting customer deliveries in 2026. That’s now 2027.
And the cash position is thin. Aptera had $10.1 million in the bank at the end of June and burns $2 to $2.2 million a month on baseline operations, according to its 10-Q, which carries a going-concern warning. It raised another $6 million through a warrant deal in July and has a $75 million equity line of credit, though drawing on it means selling shares into a market that keeps marking them down.
So even $25 million is a big ask. It’s more than a third of what the entire company is worth on the stock market today.
The product is still the good part
None of this changes what makes the Aptera interesting. It’s a two-seat, three-wheeled EV so efficient that the solar panels on its body actually matter. TÜV Rheinland measured up to 4.75 kWh a day from the integrated solar in sunny conditions, which works out to around 40 miles of daily driving without plugging in.
Top comment by Beario
In the beginning I had hopes that this concept would take off. I still have hopes that it will somehow survive, but it is looking less and less likely. It is a great concept for a super efficient vehicle, but looking at what it is up against as time goes on and as other models come to market makes the likelihood seem more and more out of reach. Still a compelling concept though that still has a possibility and hopefully things can get off the ground.
Aptera also got its EPA Certificate of Conformity in June and has ordered bodies and chassis for the first 40 vehicles. It reports about 49,300 reservations.
Electrek’s Take
We love the Aptera concept. Make a car efficient enough and rooftop solar goes from a gimmick to a real fuel source. Lightyear and Sono Motors both tried and ran out of money before getting there. Aptera is the last serious attempt standing, and the TÜV numbers back up the concept.
But a cheaper plan is only good news if someone funds it. Aptera has struggled to raise money at almost any amount for two years now, and every raise dilutes shareholders further. The market’s 15% reaction tells you investors read today’s update as Aptera having no other way than dillute their ownership in order to get to production.

title: Gazelle just made its premium electric bikes a lot more affordable
content:
Micah Toll
| Oct 1 2026 - 5:38 am PT
Gazelle has spent much of its recent e-bike development pushing its premium Ultimate platform
toward faster Class 3 commuters
, but now the Dutch bicycle maker is filling out the other side of the family.
The company has launched three new Class 1 versions of its Ultimate e-bike: the Ultimate T10, Ultimate C5, and Ultimate C380. All three are limited to pedal assist and are aimed more at recreational riders and everyday commuters who don’t necessarily need the higher speeds of Gazelle’s Ultimate Speed models.
And perhaps most importantly, they bring the Ultimate platform down to a slightly more approachable starting price of $3,499.
That still isn’t exactly bargain e-bike territory, but
has never really played in the race-to-the-bottom end of the market. These are Dutch-built e-bikes using Bosch drive systems, backed by a large dealer network, and designed more as long-term transportation than something that arrives in a cardboard box with a baggie of mystery bolts. Their high-end models have traditionally been a fair bit pricier, so these new figures are actually on the much more affordable end for anything nice enough to be badged a Gazelle.
All three new bikes use the same redesigned Ultimate platform and geometry found on the Class 3 Ultimate Speed models introduced earlier this year. That includes an active-but-upright riding position, wider tires, a suspension seatpost, and an air-sprung suspension fork. There’s also an internally mounted 540Wh Bosch battery, with the option to upgrade to an 800Wh battery or add Bosch’s PowerMore 250 range extender.
The bikes also get Bosch Smart System integration, either Kiox or Purion displays depending on the model, and Gazelle’s Intellimount system for mounting a smartphone to the stem. Integrated brake lights brighten automatically under deceleration in another nod to safety.
The $3,499 Ultimate T10 serves as the new entry point. It uses a Shimano CUES 10-speed drivetrain paired with Bosch’s latest Active Line Plus mid-drive motor, now producing 60 Nm of torque – 10 Nm more than before.
Spend another $500 and you get the $3,999 Ultimate C5, which is a new model for the North American market. This one swaps the conventional derailleur drivetrain for a Gates carbon belt drive and Shimano Nexus 5-speed internally geared hub. That’s a combination I generally prefer on utility-focused e-bikes: fewer greasy components hanging off the rear wheel and less maintenance to worry about.
At the top of the new Class 1 range is the $4,499 Ultimate C380. It also uses a Gates belt drive but pairs it with an Enviolo continuously variable transmission, providing stepless shifting instead of traditional gears. The C380 also gets Bosch’s Kiox display with onboard navigation.
There’s an interesting broader trend here, too. While much of the North American e-bike industry seems obsessed with adding more motor power, bigger batteries, throttles, and increasingly motorcycle-ish designs, Gazelle is effectively moving in the opposite direction.
These are still fairly sophisticated machines, but the premise is refreshingly bicycle-like: you pedal, the motor helps, and the whole thing is designed to feel like a really nice bicycle rather than a lightweight electric motorcycle pretending to be one.
The new Ultimate T10, C5, and C380 are available now through Gazelle dealers in the US and Canada.

title: A gas utility is picking up the upfront tab for geothermal
content:
Geothermal
Michelle Lewis
| Oct 1 2026 - 5:00 am PT
Photos courtesy of Dandelion Energy (c) 2026
Geothermal’s upfront cost can be a dealbreaker for affordable housing. A Vermont gas utility is helping get past that hurdle by paying for the underground infrastructure at a new development.
Vermont Gas (VGS) and Dandelion Energy are bringing geothermal heating and cooling to Riggs Meadow in Hinesburg, Vermont. The development will include 44 townhomes and apartments for low- and moderate-income renters and owners.
VGS will pay upfront for and own the underground pipes, known as ground loops. That takes a substantial installation expense off the affordable housing developers’ plate. Dandelion will handle the geothermal work, including system design and drilling.
Champlain Housing Trust and Evernorth, Riggs Meadow’s affordable housing developers, explored heating and cooling options with VGS before bringing Dandelion into the project.
April announcement
, VGS said geothermal would serve four multifamily buildings containing 36 of the development’s homes. Each building would have its own ground loop.
Here’s how it works
: Electric ground-source heat pumps use fluid circulating through underground pipes to move heat between the ground and the buildings. In winter, they bring heat from the ground indoors. In summer, they send heat from the homes underground. Temperatures below ground stay relatively steady, helping the system work efficiently through Vermont’s cold winters and hot summers.
The interesting part is who’s picking up the upfront tab. Developers would typically have to find the money for that underground infrastructure themselves. In this case, VGS is taking on the expense, making geothermal easier to include in affordable housing while giving the gas utility a way to offer all-electric heating and cooling.
“This partnership with utilities like VGS helps us expand geothermal access and continues to help us make this a standard, mainstream solution for developers and builders,” said Dan Yates, CEO of Dandelion Energy. “Utility-owned ground loops are a practical, immediate solution to decarbonize housing. We are proud to support and validate this model that aligns utility infrastructure investment with equitable, clean energy access.”
Under VGS’s broader geothermal offering through
Clover Energy
, the utility owns and maintains the underground infrastructure. Customers own the equipment inside the buildings and pay a monthly fee to use the ground loops, but what that fee will be at Riggs Meadow or how much residents can expect to pay for heating and cooling hasn’t yet been disclosed.
“Geothermal is one of the best solutions we have to make cost-effective, renewable heating and cooling options accessible to more Vermonters,” said Neale Lunderville, president & CEO of VGS. “We are thrilled to partner with Dandelion Energy to demonstrate ways geothermal can be scaled to meet community needs. As Vermont looks to rapidly build housing to meet demand, our teams are eager to incorporate geothermal into our product portfolio to give more choices to homebuilders and customers.”
Drilling is scheduled to begin in early 2027, and residents are expected to move into the homes in late 2027.

title: Shared grid connections concentrate battery insurance risk - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Tokio Marine GX (TMGX) sees exposures of up to billions of dollars building up at co-located battery energy storage system (BESS) sites, and says lenders are only beginning to require cyber cover.
Brian Publicover
01 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Shared grid connections at co-located solar-plus-storage sites are concentrating insured revenue into a growing risk for BESS insurers, said Olly Litterick, head of renewables at TMGX, a green transformation underwriting business that Japan’s Tokio Marine group launched in 2025.
Such projects now carry “hundreds of millions of dollars or even billions of dollars of exposure in a single location where multiple insureds share grid connection points,” he said.
Because TMGX covers loss of revenue resulting from physical damage, a failure at a shared export point can affect several insured projects at once, Litterick told
ESS News
“When the grid goes down due to [a] material damage incident or there’s a
transformer failure
or something of that description, you know, the numbers can be astronomical,” he said. “And that’s one of the many things that we as an industry need to get our heads around to support the green transition.”
TMGX acts as lead underwriter on much of its book.
“We lead, we set the terms on many of these projects and other insurers then follow us and provide additional capacity,” said Litterick. “But it’s about controlling that aggregation because these projects are just becoming bigger and bigger and bigger almost monthly.”
TMGX underwriter James Totton has also described
aggregation risk at single substation connection points
as co-location grows. In a report released in May, TMGX said the renewables insurance market must prepare for the
rising complexity of co-located projects
, with elevated aggregation risk where shared grid infrastructure creates a common point of vulnerability.
Marsh, an insurance broker, says in BESS risk guidance on its website that insurers need sufficient separation between battery modules and critical infrastructure such as site transformers and substations, and that minimizing single points of failure is key to avoiding contingent business interruption. Some insurers, including AXIS, sell contingent business interruption cover for lost income when the first substation a project does not own is damaged.
Fastest-growing line
TMGX builds on 20 to 25 years of renewable energy underwriting at GCube, which Tokio Marine acquired in 2020, covering solar, onshore wind, offshore wind, and now battery storage, mainly for property damage and resulting loss of revenue. Litterick said BESS is TMGX’s fastest-growing technology on a compound annual growth basis. He said TMGX’s figure of about 8 GW of BESS refers to its insured participation and is “probably slightly outdated” because the book is growing so quickly.
Most of that book is still in construction, he said, and utility-scale BESS has only been widespread “for the last three to five years,” so the claims record remains limited. TMGX writes significant BESS business in California but has not experienced earthquake losses. “Again, it is very, very early stage,” said Litterick.
Thermal runaway
remains the main driver of probable maximum loss estimates, and Litterick said “the spacing arrangement is obviously crucial to how we underwrite BESS.” He credited the industry with rapid progress on standardization and certification, borrowing from the solar and wind sectors. GCube reported in 2024 that more than half of BESS failures occur within the first two years of operation.
Cybersecurity gap
TMGX’s standard property cover largely excludes
cyberattacks
. Cybersecurity “is usually excluded, or there are certain perils that are written back into a general property policy,” said Litterick, with broader cyber cover usually bought in a separate specialist market. He said this leaves an uncertain gap in cover that needs to be addressed.
Project-finance lenders have traditionally required property damage, natural catastrophe, and machinery breakdown cover, Litterick said. “We are beginning to see lenders insist that their clients … purchase cyber. But it’s quite rare at the moment,” he said.
Litterick said TMGX has not really declined or repriced BESS risks over cyber exposure, because cyber cover has not been a lender requirement and TMGX has not been providing it. He added that demand from clients and lenders is rising, and that TMGX is developing a broader solution.
The cyber exposure of battery storage has drawn wider scrutiny this year. A December 2025 attack on distributed energy assets in Poland revealed a
cyber-insurance gap for battery storage
, while an EU funding ban on high-risk inverter suppliers extends to
BESS power conversion systems

title: U.S. small-scale solar adds 1.6 GW in Q2 - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Distributed solar maintained a steady deployment pace alongside 2.5 GWh of new behind the meter storage, even as a wave of thermal generation additions pulled solar’s total share of new US power capacity down to 55%.
Ryan Kennedy
01 Oct 2026
Applications & Installations
Commercial & industrial
Residential
The U.S. distributed solar market added almost 1.6 GW of new capacity in the second quarter of 2026, maintaining a steady buildout rate across behind the meter installations. According to the latest quarterly
Big Impact of Small Solar
report published by the Institute for Local Self-Reliance (ILSR), total solar power accounted for 55% of all new electric generating capacity added to the national grid in Q2 when combining large-scale and small-scale assets.
While solar retained its position as the primary source of new U.S. electricity capacity, its relative market share contracted compared to prior quarters. ILSR data indicates this dilution was driven by a sharp rise in fossil power coming online, with Q2 recording higher thermal capacity additions than any single quarter over the past two years.
Despite the headwinds created by conventional generation additions and broader market adjustments, small-scale systems continue to offer a reliable buffer for national clean energy additions. The quarter’s 1.6 GW contribution highlights the segment’s relative insulation from transmission queue bottlenecks that continue to delay multi-hundred-megawatt utility projects.
Energy storage pairing accelerates
A key factor supporting small-scale solar resilience is the rapid co-location of battery energy storage systems (BESS). Behind the meter storage deployments reached a notable threshold in Q2 2026, with over 2.5 GWh of distributed storage capacity added across residential, commercial, and community sites.
Industry analysts attribute this growth in battery integration to evolving net metering policy frameworks, which increasingly reward self-consumption and load shifting over direct grid exports. By pairing solar with local energy storage, distributed resources are providing critical grid balancing services and mitigating local distribution network congestion.
As utility-scale interconnection delays persist, the consistent deployment of small solar and distributed storage assets highlights the expanding role of decentralized generation in meeting rising national power demand.

title: South Korea grid overhaul to connect more than 100 GW of renewables - pv magazine Global
content: South Korea’s Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment (MCEE) has lifted restrictions on new renewable energy connections in the Honam region, which covers Gwangju and the provinces of North and South Jeolla in the country’s southwest. Projects already waiting for connection will get priority for early connection applications, while new projects will apply under a revised framework from January 2027, said the ministry. Parts of the Chungcheong region that were closed to new generation will also reopen, and restrictions on the east coast will be lifted in the first half of 2027, when the first phase of a high-voltage direct current line from the east coast to Singapyeong is completed. Under a new flexible connection regime, projects can connect beyond a grid section’s normal hosting limit and will have output curtailed when generation exceeds what the network can take. The ministry said this raises the solar connection limit on a distribution line from 14 MW to 16 MW and at a substation from 50 MW to 60 MW. It estimates the change will allow 2.6 GW of additional solar in Honam alone without new grid construction. The MCEE also plans to use energy storage as an alternative to new lines. By 2030, it aims to connect 3 GW of additional solar in saturated areas through storage on distribution networks and another 1.6 GW through storage at substations. The ministry did not specify the capacity of the batteries involved. It said it has already recovered 9 GW of grid connection rights by checking solar projects that had reserved capacity but were not viable. It will now also push back the connection rights of long-delayed projects to the date they will actually use the grid. The ministry said it expects to recover more than 10 GW in Honam alone by 2030 as a result, including from delayed offshore wind projects. For capacity entering from 2031, it will allocate connection rights using a 67.2% actual on-time completion rate for renewable projects, instead of assuming every project is built on schedule. Connection studies will also change. Until now, they assumed new renewable generation would run after existing fossil fuel plants. They will now assume renewables are dispatched first, reflecting actual grid operation. The ministry estimates this will allow 20 GW of additional renewable capacity nationwide by 2030, including in the southeastern Yeongnam region and northeastern Gangwon province, where coal and liquefied natural gas plants are concentrated. From January 2027, grid connection rights will be linked to a reformed renewable portfolio standard , with rights going to projects selected through competitive bidding rather than on a first-come, first-served basis. The ministry projects that the measures will raise national transmission-level renewable hosting capacity from 119 GW to 171 GW by 2030, and distribution-level capacity from 84 GW to 110 GW. In Honam, it projects transmission capacity rising from 37 GW to 64 GW and distribution capacity from 18 GW to 30 GW. Separately, the Korea Power Exchange opened a tender on Sept. 22 for 1,100 MW/6,600 MWh of six-hour battery storage under 15-year contracts. Winners are due to be announced in November, with projects to be commissioned by February 2029. Seoul-based think tank Solutions for Our Climate argued in a June 2026 paper that South Korea’s first-come, first-served queue allowed stalled projects to hold scarce grid capacity, and it called for connections to be prioritized by project readiness, with greater disclosure of congestion data. South Korea is forecast to add 3.5 GW of solar this year, according to the Export-Import Bank of Korea. title: Two-stage pyrolysis process turns waste solar panels into silicon carbide - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Russian scientists have developed a process that combines pyrolysis at 500 C with electric arc treatment above 1,800 C. The resulting solid product contained up to 61% silicon carbide, a material used in power electronics and refractory ceramics.
Lior Kahana
01 Oct 2026
Research & Development
Raw Materials
Russian researchers have developed a two-stage process to convert waste solar panels into silicon carbide (SiC), a silicon-carbon compound valued for its hardness, thermal conductivity, and resistance to heat and corrosion. SiC is widely used in applications including power electronics and refractory ceramics.
“The rapid growth in the number of solar panels worldwide is making the issue of their utilization increasingly urgent,” the researchers said. “This paper presents the results of an experimental study on the recycling of spent solar panels using pyrolysis and vacuum-free plasma electric arc conversion methods, to obtain carbon residue, silicon carbide, and synthesis gas that can be used for energy production.”
The researchers used a decommissioned polycrystalline silicon solar panel, which they shredded and pyrolyzed at 500 C under a continuous nitrogen flow to decompose its polymer components and obtain a carbon-containing solid residue.
They then processed batches of approximately 2 g of the material in a graphite crucible using a vacuum-free electric arc reactor. The reactor operated at 200 A for 60 seconds, reaching temperatures above 1,800 C.
The scientists tested different carbon additions, using carbon black to promote the conversion of silicon-containing compounds into SiC. They compared the resulting products with those obtained from panel material treated directly in the electric arc reactor without prior pyrolysis.
The researchers then used electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction, and thermal analysis to examine the products’ morphology, crystalline composition, and oxidation behavior.
“Pyrolysis helped accomplish several tasks at once: removing polymers that interfere with further processing, obtaining a solid carbon residue, and collecting gaseous products,” said Zhanar Bolatova, one of the researchers involved in the study. “According to our calculations, the average yield of carbon residue was 45.8% of the mass of the material being processed.”
Bolatova said the maximum methane concentration in the gas mixture reached 5% by volume, while carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide concentrations were approximately 0.6%.
“Analysis of the composition also confirmed the advantage of preliminary pyrolysis,” she said. “After this treatment, the iron silicide phase disappeared from the final product. This reduced the amount of unwanted impurities and increased the proportion of the target silicon carbide.”
The results also showed that increasing the carbon content of the starting mixture from 0% to 30% raised the proportion of SiC in the solid product from 46% to 61%. At the same time, the share of free silicon fell from 19.7% to 8.3%, while silicon dioxide declined from 3% to trace levels.
The researchers said the results indicate that the additional carbon promoted the conversion of silicon into SiC.
The researchers described the process in “
Stage Recycling of Solar Panels by Pyrolysis and Vacuum-free Electric Arc Conversion to Produce SiC
,” published in
. The research team included scientists from Russia’s National Research Tomsk Polytechnic University and Sevastopol State University.

title: Spanish researchers validate 10,000 cycles for iron-lead flow battery - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
A Spanish-developed iron-lead flow battery uses a single electrolyte loop and a fluorine-free membrane to cut costs and reliance on critical raw materials, with kilowatt-scale modules the next development step.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
01 Oct 2026
Research & Development
Batteries
Energy Storage
Spanish research center CIC energiGUNE has completed 10,000 charge-discharge cycles on an iron-lead redox flow battery, a design built from abundant materials and intended to store electricity for several hours in stationary applications.
The technology was tested at temperatures of 25 C to 30 C and uses iron and lead as active materials. Its single-electrolyte-loop design is intended to simplify the conventional flow battery architecture while reducing system costs and dependence on critical raw materials.
The battery also incorporates a fluorine-free membrane designed to reduce internal resistance and limit unwanted transport of chemical species between the two sides of the battery. CIC energiGUNE said the active materials have established industrial and recycling supply chains, potentially reducing dependence on critical materials.
The development is aimed at applications that require electricity to be stored for several hours, including storing excess renewable generation for later use by the electricity system.
Unlike conventional flow batteries with separate electrolyte circuits, the architecture developed by the Spanish research center uses a single electrolyte loop and fewer components.
Flow batteries store energy in electrolytes held in external tanks. Increasing the volume of electrolyte can therefore increase energy capacity, while power output depends primarily on the size and number of cells and stacks. This separation of power and energy allows systems to be configured for applications requiring several hours of storage without necessarily increasing both parameters proportionally.
CIC energiGUNE said the combination of this characteristic, high cycling capability and safety makes flow batteries suitable for solar and wind integration, grid-scale storage, microgrids and industrial energy management.
The iron-lead battery has progressed from initial laboratory cells to larger stacks. The next step is to develop kilowatt-scale modules through a combination of simulation, system design and experimental validation.
CIC energiGUNE is also researching other redox flow battery technologies, including new electrolytes and organic molecules, membranes adapted to different chemistries, electrodes, bipolar plates and stack components. It is also developing approaches to reduce the cost and vanadium consumption of vanadium-based flow batteries.
The center aims to move its developments from the materials and cell level toward complete systems through modeling, prototyping and cost and sustainability analysis. The 10,000-cycle validation represents a step toward scaling a technology designed for intensive cycling and long operating periods with reduced degradation.

title: Ireland energizes first SRESS solar farm, opening new revenue opportunities for farmers and landowners - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
“This is the beginning of a wave of small-scale energy projects being developed by farmers and communities,” Ken O’Byrne, of Flogas Energy told
pv magazine
. Flogas has a 15-year PPA with the 650 kW Meadhill Solar farm’s developer, Cork farmer Sean Keating.
Blathnaid O’Dea
01 Oct 2026
Applications & Installations
Power purchase agreements
The 650 kW Meadhill Solar farm in Cork can power around 150 homes in the locality
The first solar farm under the Irish government’s Small-Scale Renewable Energy Support Scheme (
) has been energized in County Cork. SRESS supports projects that produce between 50 kW and 6 MW of electricity.
The 650 kW Meadhill Solar farm was developed by Cork farmer Sean Keating and provides space for sheep grazing around and underneath the solar panels.
The project generates sufficient energy to power around 150 homes in the area and provides a revenue stream for Keating, who began work on it in 2017. The farmer has entered into a 15-year power purchase agreement (PPA) with Flogas, a DCC Energy-owned company that is listed on the London Stock Exchange.
Flogas is actively seeking other farmers, landowners and small enterprises interested in exploring PPAs. Ken O’Byrne, managing director, Flogas told pv magazine he sees plenty of opportunities for further PPAs under the SRESS, adding that there is a lot of capacity yet to be allocated to facilities under the scheme.
“The major benefits to farmers and communities in our opinion is to diversify revenue streams while making a positive carbon reduction impact to the national electricity grid,” O’Byrne said, pointing out that Keating’s flagship Meadhill Solar Farm project demonstrates to farmers what is achievable even on a small parcel of land.
“We think this is the beginning of a wave of small-scale energy projects being developed by farmers and communities. Significant solar deployment is occurring at domestic rooftop scale and at major utility scale. Farmer or community led projects are the scale in between these and now have the opportunity to follow suit and benefit from strong supply chains, proven solar technology and in an unobtrusive way to their farms and communities with relatively small but impactful solar installations. Farmers have been harvesting solar via crops for millennia, this is simply a new medium to harvest solar energy: via PV technology,” said the Flogas head.
Irish company PV Generation Ltd. (PVGEN) took on the installation tasks and assisted Keating throughout the development phase. Edward Carbery, the company’s group marketing lead, told pv magazine that it has been involved since the very early stages and part-funded the project.
“The planning permission and grid connection was already obtained by the client before PVGEN came on board, but we completed lots of design iterations at the pricing stage and supplied the client with production models to bring to the banks to apply for funding,” said Carbery.
PVGEN completed the electrical installation, commissioning and testing of more than 1,000 panels at the site and arranged for testing on the ground conditions, as well as for the mounting array to be designed and procured from Turkey. It also liaised with the Irish distribution systems operator to ensure the design complied with the grid connection agreement and provided the EGIP protection panel and the LV distribution board.
Like O’Byrne from Flogas, Carbery said PVGEN is seeing a lot of interest in microgeneration solar from farmers and landowners. “People are starting to see this as a good opportunity to diversify their income. We would definitely say that there has especially been a bigger interest in farmers exploring all kinds of solar projects as a result of the energy crisis and the recent jump in electricity and diesel prices.”
Besides the SRESS, the Irish government supports renewable energy generation through solar PV grants, for roof top solar on farm buildings, as part of the Targeted Agricultural Modernisation Scheme (TAMS).

title: Indian PV manufacturer Vishakha Renewables files for IPO - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Vishakha Renewables, jointly promoted by the Vishakha Group and the Adani Group, produces four of the six key components used in solar modules and is the largest solar component manufacturer (non-cell) in India in terms of combined installed production capacity as of March 31, 2026.
Uma Gupta
01 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
solar glass
Vishakha Renewables’ fully automated solar glass manufacturing facility
Vishakha Renewables Limited, a manufacturer of critical solar module components, has filed its Draft Red Herring Prospectus (DRHP) with the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) for its proposed initial public offering (IPO).
The IPO comprises a fresh issue of equity shares aggregating up to INR 1,250 crore ($129.9 million) and an offer for sale (OFS) of up to 1.82 crore equity shares by the selling shareholders. The company is jointly promoted by the Vishakha Group and the Adani Group, with Adani Properties being a promoter and a promoter selling shareholder in the offer.
Vishakha Renewables said it may also consider a pre-IPO placement of up to INR 250 crore, which, if undertaken, will reduce the size of the fresh issue.
The company proposes to utilise INR 900 crore of the net proceeds towards repayment and/or pre-payment of certain borrowings, with the balance towards general corporate purposes. As of June 30, 2026, the company had consolidated outstanding borrowings of INR 2,700.57 crore.
According to a CRISIL report, as of March 31, 2026, Vishakha Renewables was the second largest solar glass manufacturer in India, with an installed capacity of 660 tonnes per day (tpd), the second largest EVA/EPE encapsulant manufacturer, with capacity of 23.20 million linear metres, and the largest aluminium frame manufacturer in India, with an installed capacity of 14,508.75 tonnes per annum (tpa). It was also among the top 10 backsheet manufacturers in India.
The company produces four of the six key components used in solar modules and, according to the CRISIL report, is the largest solar component manufacturer (non-cell) in India in terms of combined installed production capacity as of March 31, 2026. Its four product categories collectively represent approximately 40–45% of the average cost of a bifacial solar module.
Vishakha Renewables is also expanding its solar glass manufacturing capacity from 660 tpd (equivalent to 4.4 GW of solar module capacity) to 1,920 tpd (12.80 GW), while also ramping up aluminium frame and encapsulant production. Upon completion of the solar glass expansion, the company’s facilities are expected to house the largest operational solar glass furnace in India, as stated in the DRHP.
Vishakha Renewables has entered into long-term offtake arrangements with Mundra Solar PV Ltd and Mundra Solar Energy Ltd. These include a 15-year take-or-pay arrangement for solar glass from its Phase I facility, an 8.5-year arrangement for aluminium frames and a 17-year arrangement for solar glass from its Phase II facility. The arrangements provide for minimum offtake commitments and are intended to provide demand visibility for the company’s products.
The company operates its manufacturing facilities in Mundra, Gujarat, in close proximity to the facilities of its key offtakers and the Mundra Ports and Special Economic Zone. It had 99 customers as of March 31, 2026.
SBI Capital Markets, ICICI Securities and IIFL Capital Services are the book running lead managers to the offer, while MUFG Intime India is the registrar to the offer.

title: A closer look at Marstek's 5 kWh plug-in battery - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
Marstek is targeting European markets with its Venus plug-in solution that is scalable to 9kW/15kWh. The Chinese manufacturer confirmed it is working with UK energy management providers on deeper integration to support optimization for home owners.
Matthew Lynas
01 Oct 2026
Technology & Products
Batteries
Energy Storage
Residential
Marstek Energy’s VENUS E 4.0 plug-in battery.
Marstek Energy brought its 3 kW, 5 kWh Venus E 4.0 residential storage system to Solar & Storage Live UK, Birmingham, where
pv magazine
took a closer look at the plug-in solution.
The system combines 5,024 Wh of lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) battery storage with 3 kVA grid-connected charging and discharging capability. It can also provide 3 kVA of off-grid output and deliver up to 3.6 kVA of peak backup power for 10 seconds, allowing homeowners to maintain essential loads during power outages.
Marstek Energy claims a cycle life exceeding 10,000 cycles at 25 C, with an 88% depth of discharge and efficiency above 90% across the battery and AC cycle.
According to Daisy Jiang, key account manager at Marstek Energy, the company believes the 5 kWh model is particularly well suited to British households.
“The Venus E series has already arrived in the UK through our local distribution network. Our initial focus is on the Venus E 5 kWh system, which we believe is a strong fit for the market,” Jiang said.
Designed for outdoor deployment, the Venus E 4.0 carries an IP65 rating and operates in temperatures ranging from -20 C to +60 C. The battery measures 520 mm x 430 mm x 191.2 mm, weighs 47.2 kg and uses natural convection cooling rather than active fans. Protection specifications include DC II and AC III overvoltage protection categories.
The battery supports Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, LAN, RS485, MQTT and cloud-to-cloud communications. According to Marstek Energy, these capabilities are intended to support integration with energy management systems and dynamic tariff platforms, an increasingly important feature in the UK residential storage market.
“We are currently working on deeper integration with Octopus Energy and other energy management providers,” Jiang said. “This allows homeowners to optimize battery charging and discharging around dynamic electricity pricing and maximize the value of flexible tariffs.”
Scalability is another feature of the platform. While the base unit offers 5 kWh of storage, Marstek Energy says the Venus E platform can be expanded through parallel operation to provide up to 15 kWh of storage capacity and 9 kW of power output using its SmartBox solution.
The Venus E range forms part of a wider strategy that has already seen the manufacturer establish positions in several European markets. Jiang said the company has achieved significant penetration in Germany, France, Poland, Ukraine and the Benelux countries through its plug-in storage products.
While plug-and-play batteries have gained traction across mainland Europe, UK regulations for plug-in solar introduced in August did not include plug-in battery products. The UK government has since launched a tender for a
technical risk and safety assessment
of plug-in battery products to inform future regulations.
“The deployment of plug-in battery products is currently influenced by UK regulations, which do not yet fully accommodate this type of solution,” Jiang said.
“While the regulatory environment for plug-in batteries is moving more slowly in the UK than in some European markets, we continue to see strong long-term potential,” she added. “Once UK regulations evolve to accommodate plug-in battery systems more fully, we believe the market will expand rapidly.”
Marstek Energy argues that its vertically integrated manufacturing model helps differentiate it in an increasingly crowded residential storage market. The company manufactures key system components in-house, including battery cells, inverters, battery management systems and software.
“Our biggest differentiator is vertical integration,” Jiang said. “Because we control the entire product stack, we can manage costs effectively while maintaining product quality and performance.”
In addition to the 5 kWh Venus E Gen 4.0, Marstek Energy’s full plug-in battery range includes the 2 kWh Venus E Mini, and 10 kWh Venus E Max.

title: Germany could generate over 600,000 tonnes of PV module waste by 2030 - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
A Fraunhofer CSP study estimates that Germany’s installed PV modules contain 5.35 million tonnes of materials worth billions of euros, highlighting significant recycling potential. More than 600,000 tonnes of PV waste could arise by 2030, but uncertain return volumes may create temporary overcapacity in Germany’s expanding recycling sector.
Petra Hannen
01 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
A recent
Fraunhofer Center for Silicon Photovoltaics
(Fraunhofer CSP), commissioned by the German Mineral Resources Agency (DERA), has examined the raw material and recycling potential of photovoltaic modules installed in Germany.
The materials contained in the modules represent considerable economic value, particularly aluminum and silver. According to the study, their potential material value amounts to €4.8 billion ($5.4 billion). Silver is particularly significant for the PV industry: In 2023, the sector accounted for 19.3% of global silver production.
Recycling depends on module technology
The recoverability of individual raw materials depends on the module technology and the recycling process used.
For crystalline silicon modules, Germany already has established recycling processes on an industrial scale. Glass, aluminum and copper can be recovered from discarded modules, while silver can be separated through additional refining processes.
Silicon, which accounts for a significant share of the value of some module components, is generally not recovered at present. Plastics are typically thermally treated. According to the study, current processes achieve a material recycling rate of around 85% and an overall recovery rate of more than 95%.
The study also examines thin-film modules. Cadmium telluride (CdTe) modules contain cadmium and tellurium, while CIGS modules contain indium, gallium and selenium. However, the quantities of these materials installed in Germany are comparatively small because thin-film technologies account for a much smaller share of the market than crystalline silicon modules.
Actual return volumes difficult to estimate
More than 600,000 tons of PV module waste could be generated by 2030. However, the volumes that will actually reach recycling companies, and when they will arrive, remain difficult to predict.
According to the study, the recorded volume of end-of-life modules declined between 2022 and 2024, contrary to expectations. The researchers cite several possible reasons, including the export of used modules.
Estimated quantities of end-of-life PV modules in selected EU countries, based on installed capacity (Eurostat, 2025a) and assuming a 20-year service life, an average module output of 250 W, and an average module weight of 20 kg. | Image: Fraunhofer CSP
This creates a significant gap between available recycling capacity and actual return volumes. In 2024, more than 50,000 tonnes of recycling capacity was already available for crystalline silicon modules, while only around 9,300 tonnes of decommissioned modules underwent initial processing. The study projects that recycling capacity will reach approximately 64,000 tonnes in 2026 and 75,000 tonnes by the end of 2027.
The authors therefore recommend aligning further capacity expansion with actual return volumes to avoid temporary overcapacity. Based on a modeled expansion pathway, the study estimates that annual recycling capacity of 300,000 tonnes could be sufficient by 2040. Temporary peaks in return volumes could be managed through measures such as the interim storage of decommissioned modules.

title: Second-ever reactor trial at DOME to test MW-level nuclear battery
content: A Houston startup will test an experimental “nuclear battery” in the Idaho desert next year, marking a key milestone for next-generation clean energy.The US Department of Energy selected Deployable Energy to run trials at the Idaho National Laboratory in 2027. The firm will test its microreactor inside the Demonstration of Microreactor Experiments facility, known as DOME.Deployable Energy is only the second company chosen to use the testbed. Nuclear developer Radiant carried out the inaugural test there earlier this year.Unlike traditional atomic plants, which require massive containment structures and produce gigawatts of electricity, microreactors are compact and portable. Deployable Energy’s prototype, called the Nuclear Unity Battery, is designed to generate one megawatt of electric power (1 MWe).Specific technical configurationThe machine uses a specific technical configuration: light water moderates the nuclear reaction, while circulating helium gas cools the system.“The test builds on the company’s earlier work achieving zero-power criticality through Nuclear Energy Launch Pad and will provide an opportunity to evaluate system performance, integration, controls, safety and operational procedures at increased scale,” noted INL.Officials view these demonstrations as essential for modernizing the power grid.“Testing at facilities like DOME is how we move these technologies closer to deployment,” said Chimi Zacot, acting deputy assistant secretary for Nuclear Reactors at the energy department. He added that the initiative supports the goal of providing affordable, reliable electricity across the country.Meeting technical benchmarksDeployable Energy won its slot following a competitive application window in July 2026. The testing campaign is entirely self-funded by the company.However, access to the site is not guaranteed. To keep its schedule on track, the firm must hit strict benchmarks for technical readiness, fuel procurement, and regulatory clearances.“The company must meet specific milestones throughout the process to maintain its allotted time in DOME and ensure efficient use of the test bed,” highlighted the lab.National Reactor Innovation Center (NRIC) director Brad Tomer noted that interest from commercial developers remains high.“We have a strong pipeline of companies interested in the DOME,” Tomer said, calling the momentum vital as developers push toward commercial markets.Practical engineering solutionThe test site itself represents a practical engineering solution. Located at the laboratory’s Materials and Fuels Complex, DOME officially opened in April 2026 as the world’s first facility designed specifically to run fueled microreactor tests producing up to 20 megawatts of thermal energy.Instead of building a new shell, engineers repurposed an empty structure: the containment dome of Experimental Breeder Reactor-II. The building measures 80 feet (24 meters) wide and 100 feet tall.By reusing an existing, reinforced building, researchers avoided years of construction. The facility provides private innovators with pre-built safety barriers and monitoring instruments, dramatically reducing the capital needed to collect real performance data. That data is critical, as developers must eventually satisfy strict federal regulators before any commercial reactor can connect to the public grid.
