title: US' nuclear reactor to get 190-MW more energy generating capacity
content: A Maryland-based company, Constellation Energy, has announced a long-term agreement with Amazon to support the continued investment in and expansion of the Calvert Cliffs Clean Energy Center, Maryland’s only nuclear plant and largest source of clean energy. Constellation’s new deal with Amazon is expected to enable more than $3 billion in Maryland infrastructure investment, including state-of-the-art improvements across the entire 1,790-megawatt plant and approximately 190 megawatts in total of new, emissions-free generating capacity coming online between 2030 and 2032.“This agreement demonstrates how private investment can strengthen critical energy infrastructure,” said Joe Dominguez, chairman, president and chief executive officer, Constellation.“Amazon’s commitment supports the long-term operation of Calvert Cliffs for generations to come and creates a strong foundation for future investment in both the facility and in advanced nuclear technologies.”Expansion of Calvert Cliffs’ generating capacityThe expansion of Calvert Cliffs’ generating capacity will be supported by a 20-year agreement, which includes 690 megawatts of power, including the 190-megawatt uprate. The parties have also entered into a related retail supply agreement to support Amazon operations in the 13-state PJM market. In addition to making the uprate possible, Amazon’s long-term commitment will help provide Constellation with the revenue certainty to relicense the plant for another 20 years and make progress toward the development of new clean energy power plants at the site, adding to Maryland’s supply of clean and reliable energy, according to a press release.Located in Lusby on the western shore of the Chesapeake Bay, Calvert Cliffs produces approximately 80 percent of Maryland’s clean energy and enough electricity to power the equivalent of more than 1.3 million homes. The facility employs more than 800 people and contributes about $21 million annually in taxes that support schools, roads, and other public services, according to the release.Amazon committed to investing in carbon-free energy“Amazon is committed to investing in carbon-free energy to strengthen the grid and benefit the communities where we operate,” said Kerry Person, vice president of AWS Global Operations and Data Center Delivery. “This long-term agreement with Constellation sustains the continued operation and expansion of Maryland’s largest source of carbon-free energy, supports hundreds of jobs, and brings significant new generation to the regional grid.”The companies highlighted that the latest agreement will also help Amazon manage its energy costs for facilities throughout the region. All the electricity generated by Calvert Cliffs will continue flowing to the PJM regional grid just as it does now, demonstrating how large energy users can support investments in new, reliable generation while strengthening the broader electric system.The agreement comes at a time when electricity demand is increasing rapidly, particularly because of data centers and artificial intelligence infrastructure.Large technology companies require substantial amounts of electricity around the clock. Unlike intermittent sources such as wind and solar, nuclear plants can provide continuous electricity while producing no direct carbon emissions during generation.Beyond the immediate capacity increase, the agreement could play an important role in extending the operating life of Calvert Cliffs.

title: NASA prepares humanoid robots to handle dangerous jobs on moon, Mars
content: When humans finally set up camp on the moon, they will not be alone. But will share the dusty extraterrestrial home with metallic coworkers who do not need oxygen, sleep, or coffee breaks.At NASA’s Johnson Space Center, the 16-member Dexterous Robotics Team is laying the groundwork for a future where humans and advanced robots work side by side in deep space.Science fiction has mostly imagined metallic overlords replacing human explorers. But NASA has a vastly different objective. The strategy is simple: let machines take the hits so humans can do what they do best. Robots can endure conditions that are fatal to humans, operate for long durations without life support, and reduce the massive costs and risks associated with crewed missions.“Our team is not trying to replace human explorers with robots but instead make human exploration safer and more sustainable by developing highly capable, reliable, and trustworthy robots to work in extreme environments,” said Shaun Azimi, Dexterous Robotics Team lead. “If we can send more capable robots, we can reduce the risk and make people more effective in doing the things that people do best.”NASA’s steel astronautsSpace features severe hazards like intense radiation, extreme temperatures, vacuum conditions, and destructive dust that jeopardize human survival. Robots operate without oxygen, water, food, or bulky suits, functioning reliably in these harsh environments. Therefore, assigning automated systems to high-risk tasks such as repairing station exteriors, inspecting damaged hardware, and scouting uncharted surfaces would keep human crews out of harm’s way.The team’s expertise was forged through iconic space platforms like Robonaut 2, which spent seven years aboard the International Space Station, and Valkyrie, NASA’s first bipedal humanoid. Today, those years of field experience are driving brand-new initiatives.At the center of this push is iMETRO — the Integrated Mobile Evaluation Testbed for Robotics Operations — a facility designed to bridge the gap between concept and reality. Equipped with space habitat mockups, simulation tools, and a rugged outdoor rock yard, iMETRO gives engineers and private partners a practical space to test robotic hardware and software.A major engineering hurdle for lunar and Mars missions is radio delay (ranging from a few seconds for the Moon to over 20 minutes for Mars). The software tested at iMETRO enables semi-autonomous execution, where astronauts or ground control give high-level commands, and the robot handles the granular hand-eye coordination independently.For the moon and MarsThe facility takes away the guessing game. In one test, software developed by PickNik Inc. let a robotic arm locate a spacecraft hatch, turn the latch, pull open the heavy door, and transfer cargo inside. In another project, a NASA intern built code enabling a commercial arm to inspect and maintain a station-style cold stowage freezer routinely.These trials do more than improve software. They reshape design thinking. Habitat designers are learning that small adjustments, such as adding larger handles or installing brighter lights, can benefit robotic workers just as much as human astronauts.The immediate target is humanity’s first lunar outpost, the Moon Base. But the vision stretches further out into the solar system. The team is already mapping out applications for future human missions to Mars. It will ensure that wherever people go next, their automated partners will be right beside them to share the heavy load.

title: US Air Force orders 22 more F-15EX jets to replace aging jet fleet
content: The U.S. Air Force has awarded Boeing a $2.38 billion contract to manufacture 22 more F-15EX Eagle II fighters, expanding its procurement of aircraft intended to replace aging F-15C and F-15D jets.The Lot 7 agreement was announced on September 29, ahead of the fiscal year deadline. It keeps all 22 aircraft within available funding despite the effects of production disruptions and rising defense industry costs.Boeing said the award brings the total number of F-15EX aircraft under contract across Lots 1 through 7 to 120.Keeping procurement on trackThe agreement uses congressionally provided reconciliation funding to sustain F-15EX production. According to the Air Force, negotiations accounted for the effects of a 2025 production disruption and broader inflation across the defense industrial base.The F-15 Program Office and Boeing reached an agreement that preserved the planned quantity while staying within the available resources.“Lot 7 reflects a disciplined approach to executing available resources while balancing the realities affecting defense production,” Brig. Gen. Timothy Helfrich, portfolio acquisition executive for the Fighters and Advanced Aircraft Directorate, said in the release.“The team remained focused on affordability, production continuity and delivering the aircraft needed to modernize the U.S. Air Force’s fighter fleet for the threats we face today and into the future,” he continued.The award supports near-term manufacturing while the service continues to evaluate its future fighter requirements and acquisition plans.Replacing older Eagle fightersThe F-15EX builds on the established F-15 design, introducing updated systems to support the Air Force’s fleet modernization.Described by the service as a multirole heavy fighter, the Eagle II incorporates advanced avionics, large-area cockpit displays, a digital backbone architecture, and enhanced survivability capabilities.Its intended role includes replacing aging F-15C and F-15D aircraft while providing room for further modernization as operational requirements change.Boeing describes the aircraft as the most advanced version of the Eagle family, with an all-glass touchscreen cockpit and advanced mission systems.The company’s September announcement also followed the recent delivery of F-15EX-22, the first aircraft supplied under the Lot 3 contract. Boeing said it planned further Lot 3 deliveries through the remainder of 2026 and was working with the Air Force to increase production to two aircraft per month. Coordinating the contract awardThe Air Force presented the Lot 7 negotiations as an example of its acquisition transformation approach, bringing specialists together to resolve procurement challenges.The effort involved personnel working across program management, contracting, pricing, engineering, financial management, and logistics. Their task included assessing changing production conditions and aligning the purchase with available funding.An integrated negotiation team coordinated work across these areas and elevated issues that required senior-level decisions. The service said this approach maintained accountability for cost, schedule, and aircraft quantity.Senior department leaders supported coordination and decision-making as the team worked through affordability and execution challenges before the fiscal year deadline. The latest contract sustains Eagle II production as the Air Force moves forward with replacing its older fighters.

title: 100,000-ton US nuclear aircraft carrier enters shipyard for overhaul
content: The US Navy’s nuclear-powered aircraft carrier USS Harry S. Truman (CVN 75) arrived at Newport News Shipbuilding on September 30, 2026, to begin a major midlife overhaul involving reactor refueling and extensive modernization.The work follows years of advance planning and prepares the carrier for the second half of a service life expected to span more than 50 years.Truman becomes the eighth Nimitz-class aircraft carrier to undergo a refueling and complex overhaul, or RCOH, at the HII shipyard in Virginia.Preparing for the overhaulNewport News Shipbuilding has already conducted thousands of inspections and preliminary tasks to prepare for the carrier’s arrival. The shipbuilder also ordered materials with long procurement lead times to support the project.“We’ve taken a proactive approach, from ordering long lead-time materials to conducting thousands of inspections and preliminary work, to ensure the RCOH of USS Harry S. Truman is successful,” said Bryan Caccavale, NNS vice president of program management.“This extensive engineering and construction project to ready the ship to rejoin the fleet is a team effort, across shipbuilders, suppliers and our Navy partners, and we are honored to do our part,” he added.The preparations support an overhaul that brings together nuclear refueling, structural maintenance, and upgrades across much of the ship. HII describes the RCOH as representing nearly a third of all maintenance and modernization performed during an aircraft carrier’s service life.Reactors and ship systemsA central part of Truman’s overhaul involves defueling and refueling its nuclear power plant. The project also includes major upgrades to the propulsion plant and combat systems.Beyond the reactors, shipbuilders will carry out extensive modernization in thousands of compartments and tanks, along with work on most ship systems. The scope reaches from the carrier’s internal spaces to the equipment that supports its movement through the water.Newport News Shipbuilding will blast and paint the hull and freeboard and repair the carrier’s propellers, sea chests, shafts, and rudders.These tasks make the availability a broad recapitalization effort, combining maintenance of existing equipment with modernization intended to support the carrier’s continued role in the fleet.HII said the resulting ship would be capable of supporting current and future national strategy objectives while serving as a centerpiece of naval operations for decades.Contract supports carrier’s next chapterHII announced a $5.1 billion contract for Truman’s RCOH on September 29, 2026. Options, if exercised, would raise the cumulative contract value. “Our team has been diligently working to get ahead on this critical engineering and construction project that will prepare USS Harry S. Truman for the second half of her service life,” Caccavale said in the contract announcement.“When the ship arrives at NNS, we’ll apply that same diligence to working with our suppliers and Navy partners to ensure a successful recapitalization of CVN 75,” he said. The carrier returns to the shipyard that built it. Truman was christened in 1996 and delivered to the Navy in 1998.According to HII, the overhaul will prepare Truman to return to the fleet and continue operating for decades.

title: How the world's first nuclear submarine started a new era of warfare
content: For submarines, slipping beneath the surface was only part of the challenge. The harder task was staying underwater while traveling quickly over long distances.USS Nautilus helped overcome that limitation. Commissioned on September 30, 1954, in Groton, Connecticut, it was the world’s first nuclear-powered submarine. Its arrival gave the U.S. Navy a vessel that could sustain underwater operations far beyond the capabilities of earlier diesel-electric boats.That breakthrough reshaped submarine operations, challenged established methods of hunting them, and opened a route beneath the North Pole.What made Nautilus different?Conventional diesel-electric submarines relied on batteries to power their propulsion motors underwater. Those batteries eventually needed recharging, requiring the submarine to surface or use a snorkel so its diesel engines could draw air. This dependence restricted how freely the boats could operate beneath the waves.Commanders had to manage battery reserves carefully. Traveling faster consumed stored energy more quickly, while recharging required access to the atmosphere.Nautilus used nuclear propulsion to overcome this constraint. Its reactor supplied heat to produce steam, which drove propulsion turbines and electrical generators. Unlike diesel engines, the system did not require atmospheric oxygen to generate propulsion power.The practical advantage was sustained underwater mobility. Nautilus could travel long distances submerged without repeatedly interrupting its voyage to recharge propulsion batteries.However, its commissioning and first sailing were separate milestones. After entering service in September 1954, Nautilus remained dockside for additional construction and testing. It first got underway on nuclear power on January 17, 1955.Its early voyages demonstrated the difference. During a May 1955 shakedown trip toward Puerto Rico, Nautilus covered 1,381 miles submerged in 89.8 hours. The Navy records this as the longest submerged cruise achieved to that date, at the highest sustained submerged speed recorded for a period exceeding one hour.How did it change submarine warfare?A submarine’s effectiveness depends partly on its ability to move without being located and intercepted. Nautilus gave commanders greater freedom to maintain speed underwater and quickly leave a search area.That presented a challenge for forces trained to hunt earlier submarines. During evaluations in 1956, the Navy tested how Nautilus’ increased speed and endurance affected contemporary anti-submarine warfare practices.The findings were significant: methods inherited from World War II were ineffective against a submarine with these capabilities. Nautilus’s performance required a reassessment of existing submarine-hunting tactics.Its military importance therefore extended beyond its own missions. Operating it in exercises helped the Navy understand the challenges posed by nuclear-powered submarines.The term “nuclear-powered” described its propulsion system. Nautilus carried six torpedo tubes and was not a ballistic-missile submarine.Why was its North Pole voyage important?Nautilus’ most famous achievement came in 1958 during Operation Sunshine, a mission to travel submerged beneath the North Pole.The first attempt encountered drift ice in relatively shallow Chukchi Sea waters, blocking the submarine’s passage. Nautilus returned to Pearl Harbor before making another attempt.On August 3, 1958, it successfully passed beneath the geographic North Pole, becoming the first submarine to complete that passage.The voyage demonstrated the reach of sustained underwater propulsion. Beneath Arctic ice, where access to the surface was restricted, freedom from routine battery recharging offered a decisive operational advantage.Nuclear propulsion did not make voyages unlimited. Supplies, crew endurance, maintenance, and eventual refueling remained constraints. Nautilus underwent its first reactor-core replacement in 1957 after logging 60,000 nautical miles.Its lasting contribution was giving submarines the ability to travel farther and sustain speed underwater, expanding where and how they could operate.

title: 456 nuclear reactor-powered data center in Utah proposed by US firm
content: Silicon Valley needs energy, and it is looking to turn central eastern Utah into a nuclear-powered computing capital.Energy startup Valar Atomics has submitted a proposal to construct “Project Beehive,” an ambitious industrial development spanning roughly 9,000 acres of public and state land near Price, Utah. The core proposal includes 456 small, gas-cooled nuclear reactors that would generate an estimated 9.6 gigawatts of power. That is more than double the entire state’s average energy output. Utah currently generates an average of 4 gigawatts of electricity, with summer peak demand reaching nearly 10 gigawatts.On September 17, the Utah Trust Lands Administration unanimously approved a lease for 640 acres of state trust land earmarked for the effort. The Bureau of Land Management is reviewing the project. It aims to combine small, gas-cooled nuclear reactors with manufacturing facilities to power a massive AI data center.However, environmental advocates caution against moving too fast on public land. Helium-cooled nuclear reactorsArtificial intelligence requires vast computational capacity. Computing power demands electricity. Project Beehive plans to use helium-cooled nuclear reactors instead of traditional water-cooled designs. This gas-cooling approach lowers water consumption, making it ideal for data infrastructure located in the dry American West. Moreover, the proposed complex is expected to manage both nuclear fuel production and on-site waste storage. The proposed gas-cooled reactors utilize TRISO (Tristructural Isotropic) fuel. Wrapped in ceramic and carbon layers, TRISO fuel is designed to withstand extreme heat without melting down, providing passive safety mechanisms. Valar Atomics demonstrated its central innovation, the Ward 250 microreactor, in the Utah desert roughly 30 miles from the proposed Project Beehive site. The microreactor first achieved criticality in June inside a tent structure in the Utah desert. Weeks later, during a July 1 demonstration, the firm used electricity generated by the reactor to power a single Nvidia microchip.NPR reports that non-nuclear construction could start as early as late this year, with initial reactors slated to go live in 2028.Local activists are expressing strong concern over the proposal, which joins a growing wave of data center developments across Utah. Neal Clark of the Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance voiced alarm that federal and state officials are advancing the massive project on public lands. Critics have also questioned the economic distribution. They argue that local residents bear long-term nuclear safety risks while out-of-state tech corporations capture the majority of the financial reward.Trump’s push for SMRsProject Beehive highlights the grand ambitions of a new era of companies driving a nuclear power resurgence. These ventures are supported by the Trump administration, which has introduced extensive regulatory reforms to streamline the testing and deployment of small modular reactors. Earlier, the U.S. Department of Energy selected the firm under Executive Order 14301 to achieve reactor criticality on American soil by July 4, 2026.“Under the framework of Executive Order 14301, we are part of a coordinated national effort to restore American dominance in nuclear technology,” the company stated earlier. The project now rests on federal environmental review processes.If the BLM deems Valar Atomics’ application complete, it will issue a formal Notice of Realty Action. That step triggers an environmental impact analysis under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), opening mandatory windows for public comment before any federal land leases are finalized.

title: US conducts rare nuclear blast detection test at Nevada site
content: The U.S. energy department’s National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA) has conducted an underground chemical explosive test in Nevada to study how difficult-to-detect nuclear blasts could be identified. The experiment took place at the Nevada National Security Site and was designed to improve detection of low-yield explosions linked to potential testing by China and Russia.The non-nuclear test took place inside a tunnel at the site, which is about 65 miles northwest of Las Vegas. The location was also used during the development of the first U.S. nuclear weapons. NNSA said Wednesday that measurements collected during the experiment will help scientists improve models and algorithms used to identify and characterize foreign nuclear detonations.Testing a harder-to-detect explosionThe experiment used a conventional chemical explosive, with no nuclear weapon or nuclear detonation involved. It focused on a method known as “decoupling,” which can reduce the signals produced by an underground explosion. NNSA said the test was intended to strengthen U.S. capabilities for identifying what it described as a “decoupled” explosion.The agency linked the test method to what the United States determined China conducted at its Lop Nur nuclear test site in June 2020.“Just as a stealth aircraft looks smaller on radar, decoupling can greatly muffle the signals detected by nuclear detection sensors, making a large explosion appear smaller,” the statement said.In a conventional underground test, a device is placed deep underground near surrounding rock. The resulting shock waves travel through the ground and monitoring equipment can detect them. A decoupled test uses a large underground chamber that can reduce the seismic signals reaching sensors.Sensors capture data from the blastResearchers used several types of advanced sensors during the experiment to study the explosion and its effects. The equipment included accelerometers and seismometers for measuring ground motion.The test also used infrasound sensors, electromagnetic sensors, chemical and radiotracer samplers, and meteorological instruments. NNSA said the collected measurements will support scientific models and help refine detection algorithms.The broader objective is to improve how scientists estimate the characteristics of underground explosions. Better measurements could help U.S. monitoring systems identify nuclear detonations and determine their properties when they occur.NNSA did not provide a date for the experiment.Test follows calls to resume nuclear testingThe announcement comes after President Donald Trump called for the United States to resume underground nuclear weapons testing. In October 2025, Trump said he had instructed the Pentagon to immediately restart nuclear testing on an equal basis with China and Russia.“We’ve halted [testing] many years ago, but with others doing testing, I think it’s appropriate to do so,” he said at the time.No U.S. underground nuclear weapons test has taken place since that announcement.The latest Nevada experiment does not represent a return to nuclear explosive testing. The United States has maintained a moratorium on nuclear explosive tests since 1992.

title: Boeing 777 boosts hypersonic testing capacity by 35% for US defense
content: Stratolaunch is adding a Boeing 777-200ER to its hypersonic testing fleet, giving the company another aircraft capable of carrying its Talon-A vehicles into the air.The Mojave, California-based company announced the acquisition on Sept. 30. It said the additional carrier will raise its overall flight capacity by 35 percent and expand where it can conduct missions.The 777 will join Stratolaunch’s existing carrier aircraft, Roc and Spirit of Mojave. Engineers will modify the widebody to release Talon-A vehicles through its fuselage.That work should finish in 2027. Once operational, the aircraft will give Stratolaunch another option for putting reusable hypersonic test vehicles into flight.Bigger fleet for flight testingStratolaunch has been expanding its flight operations as demand for hypersonic testing increases. Adding another carrier could give customers more opportunities to schedule missions without relying on a single aircraft.The company also expects the larger fleet to support operations from different locations. That matters for test programs that require specific ranges, weather conditions, or mission profiles.Three carrier aircraft could also support parallel missions. Stratolaunch said the additional capacity will help reduce scheduling constraints and support a higher flight cadence.The 777 brings another advantage through its size and range. Engineers can use the aircraft as a reusable first stage, carrying Talon-A to altitude before releasing it for a hypersonic flight.That approach allows the test vehicle to begin its mission from the air. It can also help researchers collect data during flight profiles that ground-based launch systems cannot easily reproduce.Talon-A is driving demandTalon-A has become the centerpiece of Stratolaunch’s hypersonic testing business. The autonomous vehicle launches from a carrier aircraft and conducts high-speed atmospheric tests before returning for recovery.Stratolaunch said it passed 10 successful hypersonic flights with Talon-A in July. The milestone came several months after the company secured a $90.8 million contract under the Department of War Test Resource Management Center’s MACH-TB program.That award covers air-launched capability test vehicles. The program gives Stratolaunch another major avenue for supporting U.S. hypersonic development.Zachary Krevor, Stratolaunch’s president and CEO, said the 777 will strengthen the company’s ability to meet customer demand. “As demand for hypersonic technologies continues to grow, we’re building the operational scale to make routine hypersonic testing a reality,” Krevor said.He added that the aircraft will provide greater flexibility as Stratolaunch works to increase its testing capacity.Another carrier enters the mixThe 777 acquisition gives Stratolaunch three carrier aircraft with which to plan future missions. That additional aircraft could become particularly useful as government and commercial programs seek more frequent flight opportunities.Hypersonic development depends heavily on flight testing and the data collected during those missions. More available carrier aircraft can give engineers additional chances to evaluate vehicles and onboard systems under real flight conditions.The new Boeing 777 will not enter service immediately. Stratolaunch must first complete the modifications needed to accommodate Talon-A and its air-launch requirements.Its planned 2027 completion will mark another step in the company’s effort to expand its testing infrastructure. Once the aircraft joins the operational fleet, Stratolaunch will have more room to schedule missions and respond to customers seeking additional hypersonic flight data.

title: High-tech computing to be tested in lunar orbit for future data centers
content: A new commercial payload agreement will demonstrate advanced AI computing capabilities in lunar orbit. Starcloud revealed that its computing payload, designated SC-1L, will fly onboard Firefly’s Elytra orbital vehicle to validate the core capabilities of a future data center around the moon that can support lunar surface and orbital infrastructure.Pairing Starcloud’s AI computing payload with our Elytra vehicle“We’re proud to collaborate with innovative customers like Starcloud and collectively take another step toward establishing the infrastructure that will power a permanent human and robotic presence at the moon,” said Ray Allensworth, Vice President of Spacecraft at Firefly Aerospace. “By pairing Starcloud’s AI computing payload with our Elytra vehicle and Solux vision system, we’re demonstrating how data can be captured, processed, and delivered from lunar orbit, laying the groundwork for the computing infrastructure future lunar operations will depend on.”Integrated on Elytra, Starcloud’s SC-1L processor will ingest data from Firefly’s onboard Solux vision system, perform high-power AI computing on orbit, and rapidly transmit the processed data back to Earth. The demonstration builds directly on Starcloud’s recent AI computing demonstration in low Earth orbit, extending those proven capabilities into lunar orbit, according to details available.Starcloud is being onboarded to Firefly’s third lunar mission that’s targeted to launch no earlier than 2028. For this mission, Firefly’s Elytra orbiter will first serve as the transfer vehicle and communications relay for Firefly’s Blue Ghost lander that will land on the Moon’s Gruithuisen Domes and operate several science and technology instruments as part of NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) initiative. Following completion of the mission, Elytra will remain in lunar orbit for five years to enable customer payload and imaging operations, including Starcloud’s demonstration, according to a press release.High-power AI computing“Space is the future of data centers, and the Moon is the next frontier for that vision,” said Ezra Feilden, Cofounder and CTO at Starcloud. “We successfully validated our ability to run and train AI models on enterprise grade GPUs in low Earth orbit, and now we’re taking this proven technology to lunar orbit. Onboard Firefly’s Elytra vehicle, we’ll demonstrate high-power AI computing and further prove we can process massive volumes of data right where it’s generated to support the growing infrastructure beyond Earth.”Formerly known as Sol3, Firefly’s Solux vision system onboard Elytra enables spacecraft to autonomously navigate, land, and track their orientation in space environments where Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) and GPS are unavailable. Elytra will also have high-resolution telescopes onboard to enable Firefly’s Ocula lunar imaging service that provides advanced lunar surface mapping, mineral detection, and reconnaissance.This will be the second Elytra vehicle Firefly is deploying to lunar orbit following the launch of Blue Ghost Mission 2, targeted for no earlier than 2027. Each Elytra vehicle is designed to remain in lunar orbit for up to five years, enabling more rapid revisit times of the lunar surface for government and commercial customers, as per the release.

title: Light-based processor targets power and bandwidth limits of GPUs
content: Q/C Technologies, a San Francisco-based developer of optical computing systems, is teaming up with a U.S. Department of Energy nanotechnology center to develop an optical processor that could eventually run artificial intelligence workloads using light instead of relying solely on electronic computation.The company announced a collaboration with the Center for Integrated Nanotechnologies (CINT) at Sandia National Laboratories to advance its optical processing unit (OPU). The proposed hardware is intended primarily for inference, when trained models process new data to generate results.Instead of performing computations entirely through conventional electronic circuits, Q/C’s approach uses the interference of light to carry out certain mathematical operations. Optical computing could potentially address power, bandwidth and scaling constraints associated with increasingly demanding computing workloads.The project remains at the research stage. Q/C and CINT will study nanophotonic components and determine which optical operations and device technologies could form the building blocks of a scalable OPU architecture.Light tackles heavy computingOne major goal is to establish a technical roadmap for moving beyond incremental improvements to graphics processing units. Researchers will examine some of the difficult problems that have prevented optical computing from becoming a mainstream alternative to electronic processors.Those challenges include performing nonlinear operations, incorporating memory, maintaining computational precision, minimizing optical losses and integrating photonic components with conventional electronics. Solving them will be important if individual optical components are eventually to operate together as a practical computing system.“Access to CINT’s scientific expertise and advanced research capabilities in photonics and nanoscale technologies represents an important step as we develop our proprietary optical computing platform,” said Joshua Silverman, executive chairman of Q/C Technologies.“As AI infrastructure faces increasing constraints in power consumption, bandwidth and scalability, we believe optical computing has the potential to fundamentally change how computationally intensive AI workloads are processed.”CINT gives the project access to expertise in nanoscience and nanophotonics at Sandia, one of the Department of Energy’s national laboratories. Sandia has approximately 17,000 employees and an annual budget of about $5 billion, with research spanning areas including microelectronics, photonics, advanced materials and high-performance computing.Building an optical processorThe collaboration will focus not only on individual photonic devices but also on determining how they could eventually be combined into Q/C’s proposed OPU. The company says the work should help identify and prioritize technologies needed for its architecture.“This collaboration provides an opportunity to accelerate our work toward a practical, scalable optical computing architecture,” said Yossef Ehrlichman, chief technology officer at Q/C Technologies.“We believe this work with CINT will help us define the pathway from fundamental optical capabilities to an integrated OPU architecture.”Q/C says its longer-term goal is to develop optical processors with substantially higher clock speeds and bandwidth while consuming less energy than traditional computing architectures. Those remain development targets rather than demonstrated performance figures for a finished processor.The company is also building infrastructure for the project. It recently established a 4,800-square-foot integrated photonics laboratory in San Francisco to support its work in photonics, computing, and the development of the OPU architecture.

title: New US facility deal targets breakthroughs in quantum RF sensing
content: A new agreement signed between an American institue and an Australian university is set to explore quantum radio frequency (RF) sensing, sensemaking, which is quantum signal interpretation and analytics, and related technologies.The new three-year memorandum of understanding (MOU) is signed by Southwest Research Institute (SwRI) and Australia-based Adelaide University.The joint research team launched first-phase, hands-on evaluations of superconducting quantum RF sensors for signals intelligence applications at the Jesper Munch Quantum Laboratories at Adelaide University in South Australia. Signals intelligence is the field of collecting, intercepting and analyzing electronic signals to support defense, communications and emergency response. “Unlike conventional antennas that get bulkier in size as frequencies get lower, quantum RF device size is independent of frequency,” said Staff Engineer Michael Quinn, who leads quantum RF research and development in SwRI’s Defense and Intelligence Solutions Division offices in Warner Robins, Georgia.“These systems achieve broad coverage, kilohertz to terahertz, with the same compact hardware. They provide more critical information and take up less space, which is a major advantage, especially for defense and intelligence missions where size, weight and power are critical considerations.”RF devices provide broad coverageThe team revealed that in superconducting materials, RF signals vastly affect the dynamics of electrons, the negatively charged building blocks of atoms. Ultrasensitive, longer-range quantum RF sensing devices use changes in electron trajectory to extract more information out of the RF environment than conventional antennas. Precision circuits made of superconducting materials produce raw data that yields accurate signal measurements. Superconducting quantum RF systems leverage the unique properties of superconducting materials, enabling highly sensitive detection and characterization of signals across a broad electromagnetic spectrum. Compact quantum systems offer the potential to replace bulky antennas, especially aboard military ships and aircraft with limited space.Adelaide University’s quantum laboratories include a state-of-the-art molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) system that “grows” advanced superconductor and quantum materials one atomic layer at a time, like a 3D printer. The MBE transforms raw materials into a Superconducting QUantum Interference Device (SQUID) supercooled to -452.47 degrees Fahrenheit to activate superconducting properties and an RF wave response, according to a press release.New material architecturesResearchers are exploring new material architectures designed to raise SQUID operating temperatures, reduce cooling requirements and improve portability and operational practicality. The collaboration unites Adelaide University’s expertise in superconducting quantum materials and sensor development with SwRI’s strengths in advanced RF engineering, signals processing and operational applications, as per the release.“The SwRI team tested and assessed selected performance metrics of the superconducting quantum RF technology developed by Adelaide University,” said Professor Giuseppe C. Tettamanzi, director of the Jesper Munch Quantum Laboratories and leader of Adelaide University’s superconducting quantum technologies research program. “By combining our complementary expertise, Adelaide University and SwRI are accelerating the development and maturation of quantum RF technologies with the potential to address the challenges of increasingly congested electromagnetic environments and complex operational scenarios. This collaboration demonstrates the value of deep scientific alliances between Australia and the United States in advancing technologies critical to future security and economic prosperity.”

title: Humanoid robots decommissioned in Terminator-style molten steel leap
content: Figure has gone full Terminator with its retired humanoid robots, sending them into a vat of molten steel.The robotics company sent F.02 units to a foundry in Imatra, Finland, where the machines autonomously leaped into a 75-ton electric arc furnace. The furnace then reduced the robots to molten metal.The unusual disposal effort followed the arrival of Figure’s newer F.03 fleet. Keeping the older robots operational no longer made sense, according to Figure. Disassembling each machine also threatened to consume engineering time needed for the company’s next-generation F.04 robot.The solution created a difficult engineering problem of its own. Figure needed to destroy proprietary hardware without exposing custom components or intellectual property. That ruled out conventional dismantling for much of the fleet.Furnace became the answerFigure eventually found a Finnish foundry willing to accept the robots. Facilities in the United States and Mexico had rejected the idea because of the lithium-ion batteries inside the machines.The company even sought help from former MythBusters members during the search. The breakthrough came after Arnold Schwarzenegger encouraged Figure to melt the robots. Schwarzenegger later joined the project.Engineers first had to teach the F.02 machines how to make the jump. Figure installed large airbags at its San Jose headquarters and trained robots to leap from a second-floor building.Stunt performers provided movement references for the training. Engineers then developed a control model in simulation. It had to guide each robot into a precise landing zone at an unfamiliar foundry.That requirement left little room for error. The team had never tested the robots inside the Finnish facility before shipping them there.Six melts, 24 hoursThe foundry’s electric arc furnace uses three large graphite electrodes to melt steel scrap. Figure had only six melting cycles across a 24-hour window.Each cycle offered roughly 20 minutes before the molten steel cooled enough to develop a solid crust. Extreme temperatures created another problem for the electronics.Electromagnetic fields also disrupted equipment around the furnace. Cameras and other electronics failed during the operation. Figure said the robots continued executing their trained movement policies despite those failures.The F.02 units ultimately disappeared into the furnace, but their material did not stay in Finland. Figure shipped the resulting metal bars back to the United States.The company now plans to machine that recovered material into a limited run of F.02 commemorative artifacts. The pieces will preserve material from the retired robots in a much smaller form.Most of Figure’s F.02 fleet has now been destroyed. A handful remain stored at the company’s headquarters.The project also served as a real-world demonstration of autonomous robot control under extreme conditions. Figure emphasized that the footage was not generated digitally. Its robots physically traveled to Finland and performed the furnace jumps themselves.Here are some of the behind the scenes for the F.02 DecommissionTo be clear: we actually trained our robots to jump autonomously, shipped them to Finland, and had them leap into a vat of molten steel pic.twitter.com/snm3Mz2v8z— Brett Adcock (@adcock_brett) September 30, 2026Figure introduced the F.03 in October 2025 as its next-generation humanoid platform. The robot features a redesigned sensory suite and hand system built specifically for Helix, Figure’s proprietary vision-language-action system.F.03 also brings changes aimed at home use, including softer exterior materials, wireless charging, and an improved audio system. Figure also made battery safety improvements for operation around people.

title: Trump unveils $200 billion US energy plan spanning nuclear, gas
content: President Donald Trump has unveiled plans for up to $200 billion in South Korean investment in U.S. energy infrastructure, including eight large nuclear reactors, a nearly 6.5-gigawatt Texas power complex and the long-planned Alaska LNG project.The package could channel billions of dollars into U.S. power generation as electricity demand rises from data centers and manufacturing. It forms part of South Korea’s broader $350 billion U.S. investment commitment tied to a trade agreement with Washington.“We’re thrilled to announce one of the largest energy infrastructure investments in American history,” Trump said.The first formal investment is a $22.3 billion combined-cycle gas power complex in Encinal, Texas. Known as Project Star, the 6,472-megawatt development is designed to deliver electricity directly to nearby data centers, with initial commercial operations expected in 2029 and the full complex targeted for 2032.Texas power feeds dataU.S. property developer Related Companies and power producer NextEra Energy will lead the project, while Texas-based Lewis Energy Group will provide the site, natural gas, water and other infrastructure.South Korean companies are expected to seek contracts covering equipment, engineering, construction and long-term maintenance.The package could also support one of the largest proposed expansions of U.S. nuclear capacity in years. Project Power establishes a framework for up to $120 billion for eight large reactors: six Westinghouse AP1000 units and two South Korean-designed APR1400 reactors.Six gigawatt power generation facility. Eight new large scale nuclear power plants. The crucial Alaska LNG plant.The Dealmaker-in-Chief, President Trump, has revolutionized American energy. The Trump Administration is ushering in a new era of American energy dominance. 🇺🇸📈 pic.twitter.com/jm2jK70ytM— The White House (@WhiteHouse) September 30, 2026Construction is proposed in three stages, while about $100 billion would cover construction and another $20 billion would be held as contingency reserves. The countries have also discussed an advance payment of up to $10 billion to secure long-lead components such as reactor vessels, steam generators and reactor coolant pumps.The framework, however, does not mean all eight reactors have been approved for construction. Individual sites, ownership structures and schedules remain undecided, and each project will require separate commercial assessments and approvals.The nuclear push comes as the U.S. looks for significantly more electricity to serve expanding data centers and manufacturing facilities. The Trump administration has also been pushing to increase domestic nuclear generation.Alaska pipeline gets boostTrump also highlighted the Alaska LNG project, a decades-old proposal to move natural gas from Alaska’s North Slope through an approximately 800-mile pipeline to a liquefaction and export facility in Nikiski.The project is designed to transport roughly 3.9 billion cubic feet of natural gas per day and produce up to 20 million metric tons of LNG annually, according to the White House. The fuel could then be shipped to Asian markets.Alaska LNG has struggled for years with financing, high projected costs and questions over commercial viability. South Korea has not given the project an unconditional green light and says its participation will depend on the economics.“It is true that the project has a weaker commercial case,” South Korean Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan said. “But from a strategic perspective, we need to examine it because South Korea’s gas supply routes are highly vulnerable.”“We have agreed with the United States that we will not proceed unless the project is commercially viable,” Kim added.Together, the Texas, nuclear and Alaska proposals are expected to account for most of the $200 billion investment commitment, potentially adding major new gas, nuclear and LNG infrastructure across the U.S.

title: Chinese lidar laser sensor detects 1,200-mph F-35 from 38 miles away
content: A Chinese missile research team has simulated a laser-based seeker detecting an F-35 stealth fighter from 38 miles away at night.The concept uses single-photon lidar to detect faint laser reflections from an aircraft. If developed into a missile seeker, the technology could offer another way to track stealth fighters beyond visual range.The research explores a sensing method that could complement the radar and infrared systems already used in air combat.Lidar targets stealth aircraftResearchers at the China Airborne Missile Academy modeled a single-photon lidar designed for missile deployment. The system operates at a wavelength of 1,064 nanometers.Lidar sends laser pulses toward a target and measures the light that returns. Single-photon systems can detect exceptionally weak signals, which makes them attractive for compact sensing applications.Missile designers face strict limits on available space, weight, and electrical power. The researchers therefore modeled a relatively small optical system rather than a large airborne sensor.The simulation used 1-millijoule laser pulses and a 100-millimeter lens. Atmospheric transmission, sky background, and detector noise also factored into the calculations.Detector recovery time received particular attention in the model. After registering a photon, the detector needs a brief period before it can record another signal.The researchers calculated that the lidar needed a signal-to-noise ratio of 8.8 decibels. A minimum of 9.4 detected photons would provide enough return signal to establish a track.Night pushes range to 38 milesLighting conditions produced a substantial difference in the modeled performance. The simulated seeker detected the F-35C from 17.2 miles during daylight.At night, the maximum range increased to 38.2 miles. Reduced background light gave the lidar a cleaner optical environment for detecting weak returns.The model also examined the quality of the target information available at shorter distances. At 17.2 miles, depth accuracy reached roughly 8 inches.Transverse resolution came in at approximately 20 inches at the same range. Such measurements could provide a missile seeker with more information than simple target detection. The figures remain predictions from a computer model.Narrow beam creates problemA longer detection range does not automatically solve the problem of finding an aircraft. Lidar relies on a narrow laser beam rather than the broad search coverage of radar.The issue matters because the F-35 already carries weapons capable of engaging targets beyond the simulated lidar range. The AIM-120D-3 AMRAAM provides a long-range air-to-air option.For closer engagements, the F-35 can carry the AIM-9X Sidewinder. Its imaging infrared seeker provides another method for identifying and tracking aircraft.The Chinese researchers chose the 1,064-nanometer wavelength partly because stealth aircraft have fewer dedicated countermeasures against active laser sensing.China has also displayed other airborne laser concepts. The 303 Research Institute recently exhibited a suspended laser weapon pod at an event in Beijing.Shenyang Aircraft Corp. has separately referenced laser weapons in design material associated with future Chinese stealth fighters.The lidar study adds another potential application for airborne laser technology. Turning the modeled performance into a practical missile system would require further development and testing.The study is published in the peer-reviewed Chinese journal Aero Weaponry.

title: OpenAI model to take on complex chip design, refine it on its own
content: OpenAI and Synopsys are developing a specialized model that can directly operate professional chip-design tools, with the goal of helping engineers move from design objectives to verified silicon faster.The companies have signed a multi-year agreement to jointly develop GPT-Synopsys, which will combine OpenAI’s frontier models with Synopsys’ electronic design automation (EDA) software and semiconductor expertise. OpenAI will also license Synopsys’ EDA tools to develop the model. Unlike a general-purpose model connected to engineering software, GPT-Synopsys is being designed to become an expert user of the tools themselves. It will learn to run EDA workflows, interpret results, and repeatedly modify designs based on those results.Engineers will be able to give the system objectives involving power, performance and area (PPA), timing or verification. Agents will then operate the tools, analyze their outputs, implement changes, and iterate toward verified results that engineers can review.Model learns engineering tools“The future of semiconductor engineering requires dramatic acceleration of the chip design process without compromising PPA or first-time-right silicon,” said Sassine Ghazi, president and CEO of Synopsys.“Together with OpenAI, we’re bringing frontier intelligence to chip design to help more companies develop and accelerate advanced silicon, while maintaining the rigor and trust required for manufacturing success.”GPT-Synopsys will run on OpenAI-hosted infrastructure and integrate with Synopsys.ai and Synopsys Autopilot, the company’s agentic engineering platform. It is also being designed to work with customers’ existing agent systems. Early technology engagements with semiconductor customers are already underway, although the companies did not name them. The deal builds on Synopsys’ broader push toward autonomous chip engineering. Just two days earlier, the company unveiled its Autopilot platform and long-horizon AgentEngineer systems, which can plan and execute multi-step engineering workflows. Synopsys said deployments of the technology have demonstrated up to 50x faster verification closure, 20 percent higher coverage and a 30 percent productivity boost.The partnership effectively aims to shift some chip-design work from engineers manually operating individual software tools to agents capable of carrying out longer sequences of engineering tasks.Agents iterate chip designs“We’re using our most advanced technology to improve the systems that power AI,” said Greg Brockman, president and co-founder of OpenAI.“With Synopsys, we’re bringing that work to chip design, helping engineers explore more designs and get to a working chip faster. By helping them build better chips, we can build better AI and bring it to more people.”OpenAI is also expanding deeper into chip development itself. Earlier this year, it unveiled Jalapeño, its first custom inference accelerator developed with Broadcom. The chip went from initial design to manufacturing tape-out in nine months, with OpenAI’s models used to speed up parts of the design and optimization process.The companies will jointly offer the compute, model and software licenses needed to use GPT-Synopsys. Their agreement also includes joint research and development, a shared revenue framework and plans to bring the technology to customers worldwide. Synopsys says customer-specific chip-design data will not be used to train the model. Data will be encrypted both at rest and in transit, while customers will have configurable controls covering retention, permissions, and auditing.

title: Bill Gates-backed nuclear fusion firm inks 6200-mile reactor tape deal
content: Commercial nuclear fusion has moved one step closer to reality. Commonwealth Fusion Systems (CFS) has signed the largest supply deal of its kind with Japanese manufacturer Fujikura Ltd. Under the agreement, CFS will purchase more than 10,000 kilometers (around 6215 miles) of high-temperature superconducting (HTS) tape to build its first fleet of commercial power stations.Fujikura is expanding its production lines in Japan. The agreement signals a critical shift for the fusion industry. Teams are moving past small-scale lab tests and assembling the industrial supply chain needed to build actual power stations.The first tape deliveries will head to Chesterfield County, Virginia. There, CFS is preparing its flagship Fall Line Fusion Power Station, designed to be the world’s first grid-scale fusion facility.Keeping the energy containedCFS’s design centers around a tokamak, which is a hollow, ring-shaped chamber designed to recreate the conditions of a star. Inside the tokamak, extreme heat and pressure force atomic nuclei together.The challenge is keeping that reaction contained. The resulting plasma reaches temperatures of over 100 million degrees, far hotter than the center of the sun, and would vaporize any physical wall it touches. Only invisible, highly concentrated magnetic fields can suspend it safely in place.This engineering hurdle explains why the Fujikura contract is so pivotal. Early fusion reactors relied on bulky, low-temperature magnets that generated modest magnetic fields and demanded sprawling cooling systems. To generate sufficient power, those experimental facilities had to be built on an enormous scale.Building stronger electromagnetsHTS tape allows engineers to build stronger electromagnets within a compact footprint. These intense magnetic fields trap high-energy plasma inside a far smaller vessel, dramatically reducing construction costs and engineering complexity.CFS is currently constructing SPARC, a prototype machine designed to prove net energy gain—meaning the reaction produces more power than it consumes. Once SPARC hits that milestone, the company plans to replicate the design at commercial scale under the plant name ARC.“This partnership with Fujikura demonstrates how we’re actively placing orders and getting ready to execute our ARC power plant,” said Bob Mumgaard, chief executive of CFS. He noted that scaling the technology requires global partners willing to invest ahead of commercial deployment.Global funding supportThe move also tightens trade ties between Tokyo and Washington in advanced manufacturing. Fujikura chief executive Naoki Okada said the deal will establish a long-term business base extending into the 2030s, when commercial fusion plants are expected to feed electricity into regional grids.The announcement caps a busy funding period for CFS. Backed by Bill Gates, the American developer recently raised $1bn in fresh capital. That round included direct investment from South Korea’s Hyundai Motor Group to explore manufacturing partnerships. With money in hand and key components secured, the company is betting that private industry can deliver clean fusion energy ahead of state-run initiatives.

title: 119 gas turbines to bring 1.7 GW of mobile power to US data centers
content: Siemens Energy will supply 119 gas turbine cores for mobile power systems in the United States, adding more than 1.7 gigawatts of planned generation capacity as electricity demand from data centers and industry continues to climb.The multi-year agreement with Dynamis Power Solutions covers SGT-400 gas turbine cores, each capable of producing about 15 megawatts. The first batch is scheduled for delivery in 2027.Dynamis will integrate the turbines into its DT18 hypermobile power packages, which are designed to bring generating capacity online faster than conventional power infrastructure. The systems can provide either temporary or permanent power.The companies are targeting data centers, oil and gas operations, utilities and other industrial facilities that need additional generation without waiting for large, fixed power plants to be built.Mobile turbines target demandThe deal comes as rapidly expanding data centers and other energy-intensive industries put additional pressure on U.S. power supplies. Mobile generation systems offer another way to add capacity where grid connections or new permanent generation may take longer to develop.The SGT-400 is a compact industrial gas turbine platform. With roughly 15 MW available from each of the 119 cores, the agreement represents approximately 1.785 GW of turbine capacity based on the stated individual output.“The demand for reliable and flexible power generation continues to grow as industries expand and energy needs evolve,” said Karim Amin, member of the executive board of Siemens Energy.“Together with Dynamis, we are helping customers access generation capacity quickly by combining proven gas turbine technology with innovative deployment concepts.”Dynamis’ DT18 is based on engineering used in the company’s larger DT35 mobile power system. The company says the new package is designed to combine utility-scale generation with a smaller footprint and faster installation.Power plants go mobileUnlike a conventional stationary power plant, the DT18 packages are intended to be transported and deployed where additional electricity is needed. That could allow operators to expand generation as demand changes or move equipment between sites.“This agreement marks another major milestone not only in our mission to deliver power where and when our partners need it most, but also to answer the market’s growing need for flexible power solutions,” said Matt Crawford, chief executive officer of Dynamis.“With ~2GW of packaged power, Dynamis has established the lead position in the hypermobile power market, and these SGT-400 packages will significantly expand that capacity.”The turbines will be manufactured at Siemens Energy’s facility in Lincoln, United Kingdom, which serves as the company’s global manufacturing center for small gas turbines.For Dynamis, the order substantially expands the amount of generation equipment available for its mobile systems. For Siemens Energy, it represents a sizable deployment of its SGT-400 platform into a U.S. market where data centers, industrial expansion, and other large electricity users are increasing demand for quickly deployable power.

title: Midair nightmare on Flydubai Israel flight: 14,000-ft plunge, stabbing
content: Flydubai Flight FZ1073 was supposed to make a routine trip from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday morning. Instead, the Boeing 737 Max 8 plunged thousands of feet after a violent confrontation erupted inside its cockpit.The aircraft carried more than 170 passengers as it crossed Saudi Arabian airspace. Flight-tracking data later showed the jet lost nearly 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds. What followed turned a normal commercial flight into a hijack scare. Israeli officials said one pilot stabbed the other and apparently tried to crash the aircraft.Passengers and crew members eventually forced their way into the cockpit. They subdued the suspected attacker and helped restore control of the aircraft.The jet then diverted to Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, where it landed safely. Both pilots went to a hospital with injuries, while Saudi authorities arrested the suspected attacker.Flight turns dangerousFZ1073 departed Dubai International Airport bound for Ben Gurion International Airport near Tel Aviv. The route normally crosses Saudi Arabia and Jordan, making the aircraft’s position unsurprising when the emergency began.The situation changed rapidly as the aircraft flew over Saudi Arabia. Flight data showed a dramatic loss of altitude before the first emergency signal appeared.The descent lasted less than a minute. The aircraft dropped nearly 14,000 feet during the initial plunge, according to Flightradar24 data cited by Reuters.That sudden change would have been immediately noticeable inside the cabin. Passengers later described screams and confusion as people realized something was seriously wrong.The aircraft also transmitted emergency signals during the incident. One signal indicated a general emergency, while another corresponded to unlawful interference or a hijacking situation.That second signal escalated the security response. Israeli authorities scrambled fighter aircraft as officials tried to determine what had happened aboard the commercial jet.Cockpit fight eruptsThe reason for the emergency soon became clearer. Israeli officials said the co-pilot attacked the pilot with a knife. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the co-pilot appeared to be trying to crash the aircraft after stabbing the other pilot.The injured pilot has since been identified as Indian national Smit Machchhar. He suffered stab wounds during the cockpit confrontation, which Israeli officials are investigating as a possible attempt to seize control of the aircraft.Passenger accounts described a chaotic scene near the cockpit. One passenger’s family member said she heard screaming before seeing a man holding a knife and a pilot on the floor.The violence left both pilots injured. Saudi officials later confirmed that the captain and co-pilot received hospital treatment after the aircraft reached Tabuk.At that point, passengers faced a problem beyond the physical attack. Someone inside the flight deck had allegedly attacked a member of the crew while the aircraft remained airborne.Netanyahu said passengers and a crew member eventually entered the cockpit. They reportedly found the injured pilot and subdued the suspected attacker.A second group of pilots also played a crucial role. Netanyahu’s spokesman said two off-duty pilots were traveling aboard the flight and later took over the aircraft.Passengers regain controlThe cockpit intervention appears to have been the turning point. Once passengers and crew restrained the attacker, the aircraft could be stabilized and redirected toward a suitable airport. The replacement pilots then prepared for an emergency landing.Tabuk became the destination. The airport’s air traffic control center received a distress call from FZ1073 requesting an emergency landing at 8:44 a.m. local time.Emergency crews prepared for the aircraft before it touched down at 9:45 a.m. The Boeing landed safely, bringing the immediate danger to an end.The passengers could not continue to Israel immediately. They remained in Saudi Arabia for about eight hours as Flydubai arranged replacement aircraft.A replacement Flydubai flight eventually carried the stranded passengers toward Israel. The aircraft later landed at Ben Gurion Airport in Israel, ending the ordeal for those aboard the original flight.❤️🙏🇮🇱 ISRAELIS HOME AFTER FLYDUBAI HIJACKING ATTEMPTAll Israeli passengers stranded in Saudi Arabia after today’s attempted Flydubai hijacking have returned home.PM Netanyahu met passengers who helped subdue the attacker.One woman recalled: “I didn’t pray for the plane to… https://t.co/E0OhbCXmRn pic.twitter.com/SrNBlvztt9— Mossad Commentary (@MOSSADil) September 30, 2026Both original pilots remained under medical care after suffering injuries during the cockpit confrontation. Saudi authorities also arrested the suspected attacker.Israeli authorities are also examining whether terrorism could have played a role. Officials have not ruled out that possibility, but they have not established a terrorist motive or explained what triggered the cockpit confrontation.The incident has left investigators with several unanswered questions. Flydubai has not established why the cockpit confrontation began, and officials have cautioned against premature speculation.Investigators must now reconstruct the cockpit struggle and the aircraft’s rapid descent. They will also examine the emergency signals and the actions that allowed the Boeing 737 Max 8 to recover.

title: Airborne robot makes soft water landing, converts to autonomous sailboat
content: Mother Nature spent millions of years perfecting the maple seed’s gentle spiral to the forest floor and the fish’s swift flick through open water. She never thought to combine them.Robotic experts at Singapore University of Technology and Design and MIT just did. Introducing ALBATROSS, a hybrid robot that leaps out of the sky like a spinning seed, splashes into the water, and instantly morphs into an autonomous, wind-driven sailboat. Short for Airborne Lander with Buoyant AuToROtating Sailing Sensor, the device offers a low-cost solution to a difficult engineering problem: building a machine that operates in both air and sea without collapsing under its own weight.“In repeated field trials at two reservoirs in Singapore, the robot sailed autonomously using a Rule-Based (RB) controller after being deployed from 150 meters in the air,” the team noted. Drop, splash, sailTypically, dual-environment drones are heavy, complex, and ruinously expensive. And require bulky motors to fight gravity in the air and separate propulsion systems to navigate currents below. ALBATROSS could change that. Instead of fighting physics, it borrows from nature’s cleverest hacks. During a 150-meter drop from the sky, its two rigid wingsails spin passively like a falling maple seed. It achieves a soft, controlled, spinning descent without relying on heavy engines or draining battery power.The moment it hits the surface, the transformation begins.Those same aerial wings lock into place as wind-driven sails, turning the fallen lander into an agile aquatic scout. Beneath the waterline, a tail rudder modeled after a fish fin takes over. When the breeze dies, the fin flicks to push the craft forward; when the wind picks up, it guides the vessel upwind toward its target.The ~1-kg ALBATROSS robot autorotates during air descent to cut its fall speed to ~7 m/s, reducing impact energy 18-fold so it survives impact with the water. Upon landing, the craft passively self-rights and transitions its dual wingsails to wind propulsion without active morphing, achieving a high 91 percent effective mass usage across air and water. In low-wind conditions, the platform drives itself forward up to 0.4 m/s through an oscillating fish-tail rudder. The design proves how recombining distinct bio-inspired components can expand operating envelopes without adding extra weight.Borrowing from nature By reusing its body parts for dual roles, the design team stripped the robot down to just three actuators and three primary sensors. It is lightweight, lean, and deceptively simple. In field tests across two Singaporean reservoirs, ALBATROSS proved it could survive high-altitude drops and immediately start sailing autonomously using a rule-based navigation controller. Computer simulations show that with Reinforcement Learning algorithms, the craft can even master complex waypoint missions entirely on its own.The development highlights a fresh approach to bio-inspired robotics. In an accompanying commentary, researchers suggest that nature serves best as a versatile library of individual biological mechanisms rather than an exact blueprint. Multimodal robotics combines diverse locomotion modes into a single platform to navigate across different environments. While animals excel at repurposing biological structures for multiple habitats, nature should serve as a flexible parts library rather than a strict blueprint. Robotics engineers can select, adapt, and recombine individual biological mechanisms to address specific technical challenges that evolutionary pressures never encountered.With climate monitoring and disaster response demanding faster, cheaper eyes on the water, ALBATROSS shows that sometimes the best way to conquer two worlds is to simply drop in and let the wind do the work.

title: Einstein Probe Discovers a Secret Phase of Neutron Star Collisions
content:
Artist’s impression of satellites observing high-energy prompt emission from a binary neutron star merger. SVOM and HXMT detected the short gamma-ray burst, while Einstein Probe captured the accompanying long-lasting X-ray emission. Credit: Yi-Han Iris Yin, HKU; reference imagery: EPSC, SVOM collaboration, NSSDC
Einstein Probe uncovered a hidden soft X-ray phase that may reveal how neutron star merger remnants remain active after short gamma-ray bursts.
A burst of gamma rays can flare for less than half a second and disappear before most X-ray telescopes have even turned toward it. For decades, that delay left astronomers with only a brief glimpse of many short gamma-ray bursts, or short GRBs. The softer X-rays released during the explosion’s earliest moments remained hidden because narrow-field X-ray telescopes generally needed a gamma-ray alert to locate the burst before repointing toward it.
Short GRBs are thought to begin when two compact stars, such as neutron stars, orbit one another, collide, and merge. The crash generates gravitational waves and produces one of the most energetic explosions in the universe, but the missing soft X-ray signal has limited what astronomers can see during and immediately after the merger.
Einstein Probe catches the hidden X-rays
Einstein Probe avoids that delay by monitoring a wide area of the sky at soft X-ray energies. On July 4, 2025, the observatory caught EP250704a/GRB 250704B as it unfolded, revealing that the explosion continued long after its initial gamma-ray flash had vanished.
An Li, a PhD student at Beijing Normal University and the Transient Advocate for Einstein Probe, was on shift when the observatory issued its onboard alerts. Li responded immediately and began a preliminary analysis.
“The event initially appeared to be an ordinary short GRB, producing a bright flash lasting less than half a second that was detected simultaneously in gamma rays by SVOM-GRM and Insight-HXMT and X-rays by EP-WXT,” said Li. “However, instead of fading away, the source continued emitting episodes of soft X-rays for nearly ten minutes.”
The prolonged emission carried substantial energy, but most conventional gamma-ray instruments would not have seen it because its spectrum fell largely at softer X-ray energies.
“Although this long-lasting emission carried substantial energy, its spectrum was so soft that, for a burst at this typical cosmological distance, it would have remained below the detection threshold of conventional gamma-ray instruments, such as Swift’s Burst Alert Telescope. As a result, previous missions would have recorded only the brief gamma-ray flash, missing the prolonged activity revealed by EP,” said Bin-Bin Zhang of Nanjing University, a co-corresponding author of the paper who initiated the detailed investigation. “Our observations show that what appears to be a typical short gamma-ray burst can actually conceal a much longer and richer episode of activity at soft X-ray energies.”
Tracing X-rays to the merger remnant
Researchers then organized an international follow-up campaign extending from X-ray and optical observations to radio wavelengths. Eleonora Troja of the University of Rome “Tor Vergata,” another co-corresponding author, led a group that obtained crucial redshift information through spectroscopic analysis.
“The coordinated observations across multiwavelengths were essential,” said Troja. “They not only allowed us to identify and study the burst’s host galaxy and measure its distance, but also enabled us to rule out an accompanying supernova and provide strong evidence linking this extraordinary X-ray emission to a compact object merger.”
The timing and behavior of the signal indicated that the prolonged X-rays came directly from the remnant left behind by the merger, rather than from the expanding blast wave. Yi-Han Iris Yin, a PhD student in the Department of Physics and the Hong Kong Institute of Astronomy and Astrophysics at The University of Hong Kong, led the high-energy analysis as a co-corresponding author.
EP250704a varied rapidly, and its spectrum changed over time. Those patterns, combined with the later behavior of the X-ray and optical afterglows, pointed to sustained activity from the central engine after the initial short GRB had faded.
“One plausible explanation is that the merger produced a rapidly rotating, highly magnetized neutron star—known as a magnetar—that powered the extended X-ray emission and continued energy injection,” said Yin.
Astronomers have searched for signals that reveal what happens during and after neutron star collisions since electromagnetic radiation and gravitational waves from a merger were jointly detected for the first time in 2017. The newly observed soft X-ray phase could provide another way to connect fast electromagnetic transients with the sources of gravitational waves.
“The newly discovered soft X-ray component provides a new probe, indicating that the fast X-ray transients are also electromagnetic counterparts to gravitational-wave sources and may originate from compact object mergers,” said Troja.
Other bursts may hide prolonged X-rays
Similar soft X-ray episodes may accompany other short GRBs without being rare. Earlier missions could have missed them because they lacked the ability to capture prompt emission below gamma-ray energies, recording only the short gamma-ray flash while the source remained active in softer X-rays.
“This discovery extends our view of neutron star mergers beyond the brief gamma-ray flash,” said Yin. “By revealing this previously hidden soft X-ray phase, Einstein Probe opens a new window for studying neutron star merger remnants and may ultimately help constrain the neutron star equation-of-state.”
“The findings also demonstrate Einstein Probe’s unique capability to uncover new classes of transient phenomena and strengthen its role in the era of multi-messenger astronomy, in which gravitational waves and electromagnetic radiation are studied together to understand some of the most extreme events in the Universe,” added Zhang.
Reference: “Minutes-long soft X-ray prompt emission from a compact object merger” by An Li, Chen-Wei Wang, Niccolò Passaleva, Jie An, Bin-Bin Zhang, Eleonora Troja, Yi-Han Iris Yin, Yuan Liu, Shao-Lin Xiong, Li-Ping Xin, Yi-Xuan Shao, Jun Yang, Hui Sun, Dong Xu, Yu-Han Yang, Roberto Ricci, He Gao, Sarah Antier, Rosa L. Becerra, Jia-Xin Cao and Bing Zhang, 10 August 2026,
